A quality engineer in a matrix organization gets conflicting priorities from her functional manager and her project manager. Keeping the matrix design, what best prevents this from recurring?
Let the engineer pick whichever request she judges more urgent each week
Agree how the two managers will share authority and settle conflicts
Route every request through the plant manager for approval first
Have the project manager set all of her priorities from now on

Dual reporting is what defines a matrix, so conflict is built in; the fix is an agreed rule for sharing authority and resolving disputes. Leaving it to the engineer pushes a management decision onto the person with the least authority, and giving one manager all the say quietly abandons the matrix.
std
I.A
A company with eight layers of management moves to a flat structure with three. Which change is most likely?
Slower decisions, because fewer managers are available to approve work
Narrower spans of control, so supervisors can watch each person more closely
Less ownership at the front line, because authority moves up the chain
Faster decisions, with each manager supervising more people
Removing layers shortens the path a decision travels and pushes authority down, at the cost of wider spans of control. Narrower spans are a feature of tall hierarchies, not flat ones.
std
I.A
A plant sets up a quality council and improvement teams that meet alongside the normal chain of command. Members keep their regular jobs. This is an example of:
A matrix structure
A functional structure
A parallel structure
A divisional structure

A parallel (collateral) structure runs improvement work beside the line organization without changing who people report to for their daily jobs. A matrix gives people two bosses for their regular work, which this arrangement does not.
std
I.B.1
A new site leader finds that most employees cannot say how their work connects to the company's goals. Which action addresses this most directly?
Add detail to the monthly variance reports each department submits
Publish a revised organization chart with clearer reporting lines
Set individual output quotas for every operator in each area
Share a clear vision and show each group how its work contributes
Setting direction and connecting people to purpose is a core leadership role, and it is exactly what is missing here. More reports, charts or quotas tell people what to do but not why it matters.
std
I.B.1
Which of these is primarily a leadership responsibility rather than a management one?
Preparing and tracking the department budget
Scheduling staff to cover every shift
Setting direction and inspiring people
Checking that work follows the approved procedure

Leadership is about direction, alignment and motivation; management is about planning, budgeting, organizing and control. Budgets, schedules and procedure checks are all management work, however important.
std
I.B.1
A CEO says quality comes first, but at every month end she pushes shipments of product that is on quality hold. What is the most likely effect on the organization?
People treat the month-end push as an exception and keep holding product
Engagement rises because the CEO is so visibly involved in operations
The quality policy gains credibility because it is applied with flexibility
People conclude that shipments outrank quality, whatever the policy says

Employees take their cue from what leaders do under pressure more than from what they say, so the real priority becomes shipping. Treating it as an exception is the hopeful reading, but a repeated pattern teaches the opposite.
std
I.B.2
A manager compares weekly scrap against the target and starts corrective action whenever it goes over the limit. Which management function is this?
Planning
Organizing
Coordinating
Controlling
Controlling means measuring results, comparing them with the standard and correcting deviations. Planning set the scrap target in the first place, but acting on the gap is control.
std
I.B.2
A newly promoted production manager keeps fixing equipment problems himself while schedules slip and his team waits for direction. Which competency gap is most evident?
Delegating and coordinating the work of the team
Technical knowledge of the process equipment
Understanding the product's design requirements
Willingness to work alongside people on the floor

As people move into management, their value shifts from doing technical work to getting work done through others. His technical skill is clearly strong; what is missing is assigning the work and coordinating the team.
std
I.B.2
Which activity is an example of a manager's organizing function?
Grouping tasks into jobs and assigning authority and resources
Setting the department's annual objectives and targets
Comparing results with targets and correcting deviations
Coaching employees one on one to help them improve their performance
Organizing arranges people, tasks, authority and resources so the plan can be carried out. Setting objectives is planning, comparing results is controlling, and coaching belongs to leading.
std
I.B.3
Operators are resisting a new electronic inspection system. Interviews show they fear the data will be used to discipline them. What should the change leader do first?
Delay the rollout until next year so that the concerns have time to fade away
Announce that the system is mandatory and that use will be audited
Explain how the data will be used and involve operators in setting the rules
Offer a bonus to the first operators who adopt the new system

Resistance is best handled by addressing its actual cause, here a fear of misuse, and participation builds commitment. Mandating use or paying for it leaves the fear in place and tends to drive resistance underground.
std
I.B.3

Training on a new method went well and it was used for several weeks, but no one updated the standard work, audits or performance measures. Six months later people have drifted back to the old way. Which stage of Lewin's change model was neglected?
Unfreezing
Refreezing
Moving
Planning
Refreezing locks in the new behavior through standards, measures, audits and rewards; without it people slide back. The weeks of successful use show that unfreezing and moving did happen.
std
I.B.3
A quality manager wants to understand a plant's real quality culture. Which source gives the most reliable evidence?
The quality policy posted in the lobby and on the company intranet
The values statement published in the most recent annual report
How managers answer an employee survey question about their quality priorities
What people do, and what gets rewarded, when quality and output conflict

Culture lives in shared assumptions that show up in behavior and in what the organization rewards, especially when goals collide. Policies, value statements and survey answers show espoused values, which may differ from the real ones.
std
I.B.3
A company certified to ISO 9001 acquires a firm whose quality system and culture are quite different. What should the quality leader do first?
Replace the acquired firm's procedures with the buyer's within the first month
Leave the acquired firm's system alone until its next customer audit
Assess both systems and cultures for gaps, risks and practices to keep
Move the buyer's quality staff in to run the acquired firm's sites

Integration decisions should rest on an assessment of both systems and cultures, since the acquired firm may have strengths and customer obligations of its own. Imposing procedures at once ignores culture and risks losing what works, while waiting for an audit leaves the risks unmanaged.
std
I.B.4
A plant raised wages and improved working conditions, but engagement scores did not improve. According to Herzberg, what should leaders focus on next?
Recognition, achievement, responsibility and meaningful, challenging work
Further gains in pay, benefits and physical working conditions
Closer supervision so that good performance is noticed sooner
Clearer attendance rules and consistent discipline for absence

Herzberg found that hygiene factors such as pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate; motivators come from the work itself. More pay and better conditions are the hygiene factors that have already been tried.
std
I.B.4
Production wants to reduce final inspection to meet demand; quality wants it kept as is. A manager is asked to help them reach a lasting agreement. Which approach fits best?
Explore each side's needs and seek options that meet both
Split the difference by cutting the inspection effort in half
Ask each side to restate its position until one of them concedes
Escalate to the general manager and have him make the decision

Interest-based negotiation looks past stated positions to the underlying needs, here throughput and assurance of conformance, and searches for options serving both. Splitting the difference is a compromise that may satisfy neither need and does not last.
std
I.B.4
A team is convinced a supplier caused a defect, though its data are thin. The leader wants members to examine their own reasoning rather than be told they are wrong. Which technique fits?
Socratic questioning on how they know and what would change their view
Brainstorming to generate a longer list of other possible causes of the defect
Multivoting so the team can settle on the cause most members believe is likely
Using positional authority to overrule the team and assign a new direction

Socratic questioning leads people to test their own assumptions and evidence, so the conclusion is theirs. Brainstorming widens the list of causes but does not challenge the reasoning behind the favored one, and voting only counts beliefs.
std
I.B.4
A quality manager needs a peer department head to adopt a new process check. She has no authority over him. Which approach is most likely to gain his support?
Ask the CEO to direct him to comply with the new check
Implement the check in his area and report results later
Send him the clause of the standard that requires the check and ask him to comply
Show how the check helps his own goals and build on shared interests

Influence without authority works by connecting the request to what the other person cares about. Going over his head or around him may get compliance once but damages the relationship, and citing a clause rarely changes anyone's mind.
std
I.B.5
An assembler who installed one component now also installs two others that need the same skill level. This change is:
Job enlargement
Job enrichment
Job rotation
Job specialization
Adding more tasks at the same level widens the job horizontally, which is enlargement. Enrichment would add depth, such as planning, decision making or responsibility for quality.
std
I.B.5
Which change is an example of job enrichment for a machine operator?
Authority to plan the work, check quality and stop the machine
Running a second machine of the same type alongside the first
Moving among three workstations every two hours during the shift
Earning a higher hourly rate after completing a skills review
Enrichment adds vertical depth: planning, control and decision authority that used to sit above the job. Running a second identical machine adds more of the same work, which is enlargement.
std
I.B.5
Management announces that teams are empowered to solve problems, but every proposal still needs three signatures and teams cannot see cost data. What is the main obstacle to empowerment?
The teams lack the motivation needed to take on problem solving
The teams are too large to reach decisions in a reasonable time
The teams have responsibility without the authority or information to act
The teams have not been given clear targets for the problems they are asked to solve
Empowerment requires authority and information to match the responsibility; the signatures and hidden data withhold both. Nothing in the situation points to a motivation or team-size problem.
std
I.C.1
Engineers in three countries work together on a design through video calls and shared files and almost never meet in person. This is a:
Self-managed team
Work group
Process improvement team
Virtual team

A virtual team works across distance mainly through technology. Nothing indicates the team manages itself or is improving a process, and members working toward a shared design is a team, not a work group.
std
I.C.1
Operators in a cell schedule their own work, assign tasks among themselves and run their own quality checks, with no supervisor. This is a:
Process improvement team
Temporary (ad hoc) team
Virtual team
Self-managed team

A self-managed team takes on responsibilities a supervisor would normally hold and is part of the ongoing structure. A process improvement team is formed to improve a specific process and is not responsible for running the daily work.
std
I.C.1
Which situation describes a work group rather than a team?
Members share one goal and hold one another accountable for the result
Members come from several functions to improve one shared process
Members report to one supervisor and pursue their own individual goals
Members manage their schedules and divide the tasks among themselves
A work group is people who share a boss or location but work toward individual goals. A team, by contrast, has a common purpose and mutual accountability, which every other option describes.
std
I.C.2
Two weeks after launch, team members argue about the approach and openly challenge the leader. What stage is this, and what should the leader do?
Forming; give detailed direction and hold more introductions and icebreakers
Storming; surface the conflict and help the team agree how to work
Norming; step back and let members take over leadership of the meetings
Performing; delegate fully and focus on the team's long-range direction

Conflict over approach and authority marks storming, and the leader's job is to surface and resolve it so the team can agree on norms. Stepping back belongs to later stages, once the team has settled how it will work.
std
I.C.2
A newly formed team is polite, unsure of its purpose and looks to the leader for direction. Which leadership style fits best?
Delegating: let members work out their own purpose and goals
Directive: clarify the purpose, goals, roles and ground rules
Supportive: focus mainly on settling interpersonal conflicts
Hands-off: wait for natural leaders within the team to emerge
In forming, members need structure and clarity, so a directive style fits. Delegating suits a performing team, and there is no conflict yet to settle.
std
I.C.2
A team works smoothly, members settle disagreements themselves and results are strong. How should the leader adjust?
Give closer direction to keep up the team's momentum
Delegate more and focus on removing obstacles
Restate the ground rules so that standards do not slip
Take back decisions so the team stays focused on results
A performing team needs little direction; the leader adds most value by delegating, removing barriers and looking ahead. Closer direction at this stage slows the team down and signals distrust.
std
I.C.3
A cross-functional team meets for the first time. Members come from four departments, and several have never met. What should the leader do first?
Run introductions so members learn each other's skills
Assign data collection tasks so the work can begin right away
Present the leader's proposed solution for the team to refine
Set the date for the team's final presentation to management

Introductions and ice-breakers build the relationships and awareness of skills a team needs before it can work well. Jumping into tasks skips that foundation, and presenting a solution undercuts the team's reason for existing.
std
I.C.3
Halfway through a project, team members are pulling in different directions, each pursuing what their own department wants. Which launch step was most likely skipped?
Training members in problem-solving tools
Setting the meeting schedule and location
Assigning a timekeeper and note-taker
Agreeing on a shared vision and goals

Without a common vision and agreed objectives, members default to their departments' goals. Tool training and meeting logistics matter, but they do not align people on what the team is trying to achieve.
std
I.C.3
Team meetings run long, action items are dropped, and no one is sure who should update the sponsor. What is the most direct fix?
Add more members so that the work is spread across more people
Hold meetings twice as often until the action backlog is cleared
Assign clear roles and an owner and due date for each action
Ask the sponsor to attend every meeting and take the notes
The symptoms point to unclear roles and accountability, which assigning roles and owners fixes directly. More members or more meetings add effort without fixing who is responsible for what.
std
I.C.4
Which team role is a senior manager who sponsors the project, provides resources and removes organizational barriers?
Facilitator
Process owner
Champion
Team leader
The champion (sponsor) supports the team from above with resources and authority. The team leader runs the team's work day to day but usually cannot clear barriers across the organization.
std
I.C.4
After an improvement project closes, who is responsible for sustaining the improved process and its controls?
The champion
The process owner
The facilitator
The project team leader
The process owner manages the process day to day and owns its performance after the project team disbands. The champion sponsored the project but does not run the process.
std
I.C.4
A team member keeps steering discussion away from one possible cause, which involves his own department. What should the team leader do?
Remove him from the team at once and replace him with a colleague
Raise the concern with him privately and bring the team back to the data
Let it go so as not to create conflict within the team this early
Ask the team to vote on whether he is biased toward his own department's interests

A suspected hidden agenda is best addressed directly but privately, while the team keeps its decisions grounded in data. Ignoring it lets the agenda steer the outcome, and a public vote would humiliate him and damage the team.
std
I.C.4
Two team members argue in every meeting, and the disagreement has become personal. What should the team leader do first?
Let the team vote on which member's position is correct and move on
Report both members to their managers so discipline can be applied
Meet with both and use the ground rules to agree how to work together
Keep them on separate tasks and avoid mentioning the conflict at all

Conflict that has turned personal needs to be addressed directly with the people involved, using the team's agreed norms. A vote settles nothing about the relationship, and avoidance lets it keep damaging the team.
std
I.C.5
A team met its scrap reduction target, but members note that only the leader was thanked at the all-hands meeting. What should management do?
Give the leader a larger bonus to share out as he sees fit
Recognize the whole team soon, citing specific contributions
Recognize individual members at their next annual reviews
Post the results without names to avoid any favoritism

Recognition works best when it is timely, specific and given to everyone who earned it. Waiting for annual reviews breaks the link between the result and the reward, and anonymous posting recognizes no one.
std
I.C.5
A team chartered to cut late deliveries by 30% reports that it held every meeting, finished its training and completed its process map on time. What should the sponsor ask for?
Data on the change in late deliveries measured against the 30% goal
A record of attendance at each of the team's meetings so far
Feedback from members on how well the team is working together
A summary of the training modules each member has completed
A team is evaluated against the metrics in its charter, and everything reported so far is activity rather than result. Team health feedback is useful but does not show whether the goal is being met.
std
I.C.5
A team is midway through a nine-month improvement project. When is recognition most appropriate?
When it reaches key milestones or meaningful interim results
Only at completion, so it does not distract from the work
Only if the final result exceeds the target in the charter
At every meeting, whether or not progress has been made

Celebrating real milestones sustains energy over a long project and reinforces the behaviors that produced progress. Waiting until the end loses months of motivation, while praise unrelated to progress loses its meaning.
std
I.D.1
A quality manager is asked by her vice president to sign a test report that she knows leaves out failed results so a product can ship. What should she do?
Sign it but keep a private record of the results that were left out
Sign it, since the vice president is accountable for the decision
Sign it if the customer did not specifically ask for those tests
Refuse to sign and report the omission through the proper channels
Signing a report known to be misleading violates the duty of honesty and puts users at risk, regardless of who ordered it. Keeping a private record does not make the signed report honest.
std
I.D.1
An auditor is assigned to audit a supplier owned by his brother-in-law. What should he do?
Do the audit, grading more strictly to offset any bias
Do the audit, disclosing the tie only if challenged
Disclose the relationship and ask to be reassigned to another audit
Do the audit, since his training ensures objectivity
A conflict of interest should be disclosed and avoided, not managed privately by the person who has it. Grading more strictly is still biased judgment, just in the other direction.
std
I.D.1
A client asks a quality consultant to lead a statistical validation that is well beyond her training and experience. What should she do?
Accept the work and learn the methods as she goes without telling anyone
Accept the work and add a disclaimer about her experience to the report
Tell the client the limits of her expertise and involve a qualified person
Decline all further work for this client to avoid any future problems

Professionals should take on only work they are competent to perform and be open about their limits. A disclaimer in the final report comes too late and does not make the work sound, while refusing all future work is an overreaction.
std
I.D.2
During a supplier selection, a bidder's sales representative offers a quality engineer an all-expenses-paid resort trip. What should the engineer do?
Decline it and report the offer, as company policy on gifts requires
Accept it if he declares it after the contract has been awarded
Accept it if the bidder offers the same trip to his colleagues
Accept it but score that bidder strictly to offset any bias

A valuable gift from a bidder during selection is a bribery and conflict-of-interest risk and should be refused and reported. Declaring it after the award does not undo the influence it may have had on the decision.
std
I.D.2
Which is an example of the governance element of ESG (environmental, social and governance)?
Reducing greenhouse gas emissions and waste from the plant
Workplace safety and fair labor practices in the supply chain
Community investment and employee volunteering programs
Board oversight, executive accountability and anti-corruption controls

Governance covers how the company is directed and controlled: board oversight, ethics, anti-corruption and accountability. Labor practices and safety fall under the social element, and emissions under environmental.
std
I.D.2
A supervisor tells operators to bypass a machine guard to recover lost output. The quality manager learns of it. What should the quality manager do?
Allow it for this shift and record the bypass as a deviation
Stop the practice and escalate it as a safety compliance issue
Raise it at next month's safety meeting for discussion
Leave it to the safety department, since it is not quality
Bypassing a guard is an immediate safety and regulatory hazard that any manager has a duty to stop and escalate. Waiting for the monthly meeting leaves people exposed in the meantime.
std
I.D.3
An engineer wants to send proprietary process drawings to a prospective supplier so it can quote the job. What should be in place first?
A quality agreement that defines the inspection requirements
A signed non-disclosure agreement covering the drawings
A purchase order for the first production lot of the part
A completed supplier self-assessment questionnaire on file

A non-disclosure agreement protects the company's intellectual property before it is shared. A quality agreement governs requirements once the supplier is producing and is not the instrument for protecting information at the quoting stage.
std
I.D.3
A supplier changed its resin source without telling the customer, and parts later failed in the field. Which agreement would most directly have prevented this?
A non-disclosure agreement covering the customer's drawings and specifications
One requiring advance notice and approval of material or process changes
A certificate of conformance supplied with each lot shipped to the customer
A pricing agreement that commits the supplier to annual cost reductions

A change notification clause, usually in the quality agreement, obliges the supplier to inform the customer and get approval before changing materials or processes. A certificate of conformance only attests that a lot meets the specification, and it would not reveal a change in source.
std
I.D.3
A quality engineer sees records being altered to hide that a product failed a regulatory test. The company has an ethics hotline. What should she do?
Document what she observed and report it through the hotline
Confront the employees and demand that they correct the records
Post the evidence publicly so that customers are warned at once
Wait to see whether the product causes any problems in the field

Suspected illegal activity should be documented factually and reported through the designated channel, which protects both the investigation and the reporter. Confronting the people involved can lead to destroyed evidence and retaliation.
std
II.A
A leadership team adopts the statement: “To be the most trusted supplier of medical tubing in North America.” This statement is best classified as the organization's:
Vision statement
Mission statement
Values statement
Strategic objective

A vision describes the future state the organization aspires to reach. A mission states the organization's purpose today (what it does and for whom), and an objective would carry a measure and a date.
std
II.A
A new leadership team has confirmed its mission, vision and values and is ready to continue strategic planning. What should it do next?
Assign action plans and owners to each department
Set next year's budget for each improvement project
Analyze the internal and external environment
Select the measures for the balanced scorecard first

Strategic objectives should rest on an assessment of the environment (for example SWOT), so the scan comes before objectives, tactics, budgets and measures. Assigning action plans now would deploy tactics before anyone knows what the strategy is.
std
II.A

A company's stated values include “the customer's voice comes first.” Complaint responses average 45 days, and management has not reviewed the complaint backlog in a year. What does this most clearly show?
The company's mission statement must be rewritten
Its values are not yet guiding daily decisions
The complaint target should be dropped from the plan
The complaint process owner's objectives fail the SMART test

Values only work as guiding principles when they govern how people actually spend time and attention, and here complaints sit unanswered. The mission (the organization's purpose) is not what failed, so rewriting it would not address the gap.
std
II.A
A hospital's mission is to provide safe, compassionate care to its community. Which proposed strategic objective is most clearly linked to that mission?
Double revenue from elective cosmetic procedures
Open a retail pharmacy in a neighboring state
Move the billing office into a lower-cost building
Cut hospital-acquired infections 30% in two years
Hospital-acquired infections are a direct measure of safe care for the community the mission names. The other objectives may help finances, but none ties to safety, compassion or the local community.
std
II.B.1
During a SWOT session, a team lists “our scrap rate is twice the industry average.” Where does this item belong?
Threat, because it endangers future profit
Weakness, as it is internal to the firm
Opportunity, since projects can improve it
Strength, since the data are already known

SWOT separates internal factors (strengths and weaknesses) from external ones (opportunities and threats). High scrap is an internal condition the firm controls, so it is a weakness even though it hurts profit the way a threat would.
std
II.B.1
A plant's PESTLE analysis notes that skilled machinists are retiring faster than the local schools can train replacements. Which PESTLE factor does this fall under?
Economic
Political
Social
Technological
Workforce demographics and education are social factors. The shortage will raise labor costs, which tempts an economic label, but the driver itself is a change in the population and its skills.

II.B.1

Threat of substitutes

Buyer power; sign longer contracts with customers
Supplier power; qualify an alternate source or resin

Which condition most reduces the threat of new competitors entering an industry?
Many small firms selling similar products
Customers can change suppliers at little cost
Industry profits are well above average
Heavy capital and certification requirements
High capital needs and certification requirements are barriers to entry that keep newcomers out. Above-average profits do the opposite: they attract entrants.

Manage closely with frequent involvement
Keep informed with regular updates
Monitor with minimal communication
Keep satisfied without overloading them

High-power, low-interest stakeholders are kept satisfied so their interest does not turn into opposition. Close management is reserved for those high on both power and interest; monitoring alone ignores the regulator's power.

Rank objectives by shareholder priority, since owners bear the risk
Set a separate objective for each group and let them compete for funding
Find objectives that serve several groups at once and state the tradeoffs openly
Leave employee needs to HR policy and plan around customers and owners

Needs of other stakeholders are missed, inviting later resistance
The plan will lack enough financial analysis to win approval
Executives will reject the plan as too detailed to act upon
Community groups will be consulted too early and stall the plan

Autonomation
Automation
Cloud computing
Total productive maintenance

Autonomation (jidoka, automation with a human touch) builds in the ability to detect an abnormality and stop, so defects are not passed on. Plain automation runs the task but does not judge its own output.

Whether the move lowers server hardware costs
Whether its controls meet legal and customer terms
Whether staff will prefer the new user interface
Whether the provider can add AI features later on

Customer agreements and laws set obligations for where and how that data is protected, so the provider's security and data-location controls decide whether the move is allowed at all. Hardware savings matter only once compliance is settled.

A plant wants an AI vision system to make accept/reject decisions at final inspection. Which issue most directly affects compliance with its quality system?
The system must have a faster cycle time than human inspectors
The vendor must already supply other plants in the same industry
The model must be validated and changes to it must be controlled
The project must be funded from the information technology budget

An AI model making product decisions is an inspection method, so it needs to be shown capable and kept under change control like any other. Faster cycle time is a business benefit, not a conformance requirement.

A strategy calls for 40% more unit volume within two years. The bottleneck line already runs three shifts, seven days a week, at 90% utilization. What does this tell the planners?
The target needs added capacity at the bottleneck line
The line can absorb the growth with some overtime
The utilization figure means the line is underused
Non-bottleneck lines should be sped up right away

The growth needs about 126% of the bottleneck's current capacity (0.90 x 1.40), and a line already running around the clock has no overtime left, so capacity must be added or the bottleneck improved for the target to be credible. Speeding up non-bottleneck lines does not raise system output.

A firm's strategy is to enter the aerospace market, which requires certified nondestructive testing staff. It has none. What should the internal capability analysis lead to?
Entering the market now and certifying staff later
Removing aerospace from the strategy altogether
Hiring or training certified staff, with lead time
Asking customers to waive the requirement for now

A capability gap in people should become part of the plan, with the time it takes to hire or certify built into the launch date. Entering first would mean shipping work the firm is not qualified to perform.

Which tool compares the capabilities a strategy requires with the capabilities an organization has now?
Gap analysis
PESTLE analysis
Pareto chart
Five forces analysis
Gap analysis sets the required state against the current state to show what must be built. PESTLE and five forces look outward at the environment and the industry, not at internal capability.

An industry association standard has no legal force, but the largest customers require suppliers to conform to it. How should the strategic plan treat it?
As optional, since no law makes it mandatory
As a requirement for keeping key customers
As a matter for the legal team rather than planners
As a goal to revisit once current laws are met

A standard customers demand works as a condition of doing business, whatever its legal status, so the plan must account for it. Treating it as optional because it is not a law could cost the firm its biggest accounts.

II.B.6
A regulation taking effect in three years will ban a substance used in several of a company's products. How should this shape the strategic plan?
Wait for the final enforcement guidance
Plan to request an exemption for all products
Build redesign and requalification into it
Shift the issue to suppliers to resolve alone

A known future requirement should be built into the plan with milestones for redesign, supplier changes and requalification ahead of the effective date. Waiting for guidance consumes lead time the transition needs.

II.B.6
Recommended industry best practices differ from regulations in that best practices:
Are voluntary unless a contract or law adopts them
Are enforced by government inspectors and fines
Apply only to firms that belong to the association
Cannot be audited by customers or registrars

Best practices and consensus standards are voluntary on their own, but they become binding when a contract or a regulation references them. Government enforcement is what defines a regulation, not a best practice.

Greatly improve customer satisfaction across the business this year
Reach zero defects at every plant starting at the beginning of next month
Reduce scrap on all product lines as much as current resources will allow
Cut Line 3 changeover time from 90 to 45 minutes by June 30

The changeover tactic names a specific line, a measurable change, a feasible target and a date, and cutting changeover time frees capacity, so it is relevant to the objective. A proposed tactic reads: “Install the new scheduling module in the ERP system by September 30.” Which question best tests whether it is relevant?
Can the IT team finish the installation on time
Which of our strategic objectives will this module advance
How many users will need training on the module
What will the module's annual license fee be
Relevance in SMART means the tactic connects to a strategic objective. Whether IT can finish on time tests attainability, not relevance.

II.C.1
A strategic objective is to cut customer complaints 25%. A department's tactic is “Train 100% of operators in SPC by December.” What is the main weakness of this tactic?
It has no completion date that can be tracked
Its target of 100% cannot possibly be attained
Its link to fewer complaints is not shown
It is too narrow to be called a specific tactic

The tactic is specific, measurable and dated, but it counts training activity, and nothing shows SPC training addresses the causes of complaints. December is a trackable deadline, so the time criterion is met.

A plant launched five strategic initiatives, all staffed by the same three engineers on top of their daily work. Six months in, all five are behind. What should the leadership team do first?
Add weekly status meetings for all five projects
Replace the engineers with a stronger project team
Extend every deadline by six months to reduce stress
Prioritize and match initiatives to real capacity

The problem is demand exceeding capacity, so leaders must rank the initiatives and resource or defer them to fit. More status meetings take more time from the same overloaded people without adding any capacity.

Improvement teams need four signatures for any purchase over $200, which delays kaizen events by weeks. What should the quality manager do?
Have teams submit purchases weeks before each event
Pay for the small purchases personally and claim them
Cancel kaizen events that require any purchasing
Work with finance on a faster path for approved work

Removing administrative barriers to strategic initiatives is a leadership job, and a controlled fast path keeps financial control while letting the work proceed. Planning further ahead works around the barrier but leaves it in place for everyone else.

II.C.2
A survey after deployment finds most supervisors cannot explain how their department goals connect to the strategic plan. What is the best response?
Post the full strategic plan on the intranet for all
Cascade the plan in their terms and check understanding
Remove department goals until the next planning cycle
Tie supervisor bonuses to the company's annual profit

People can only carry out a plan they understand, so leaders should explain the links in terms of each department's work and check that the message landed. Posting the document on the intranet is one-way communication: it does not translate the plan into department terms or confirm that anyone understood it.

A balanced scorecard balances financial measures with which three other perspectives?
Customer, supplier, and regulatory compliance risk
Quality, delivery, and cost of operations
Customer, internal process, learning and growth
Employee, community, and environmental impact

Kaplan and Norton's balanced scorecard adds customer, internal business process, and learning and growth perspectives to the financial one. Quality, delivery and cost are common operational measures but are not the scorecard's perspectives.

Which of these is a leading indicator rather than a lagging one?
Annual warranty cost as a percentage of sales
Customer churn rate for the last quarter
Return on assets at the end of the fiscal year
Preventive maintenance completed on schedule
Completing preventive maintenance is a driver that predicts future equipment performance, so it leads. Warranty cost, churn and return on assets report what has already happened.

Purchasing is measured on unit price savings, while the strategic goal is lower total cost and better quality. Buyers switch to a cheaper supplier and incoming rejects rise. What does this show?
The supplier quality engineer did not audit the supplier
Buyers were not trained in reading the strategic plan
Incoming inspection needs to sample more heavily
The purchasing measure drives behavior against the goal

Measures shape behavior, and a unit-price measure rewarded a choice that raised total cost. More incoming inspection would catch more rejects but leave the misaligned measure, and its cause, in place.

In hoshin kanri, the back-and-forth discussion in which managers at adjacent levels negotiate targets and the means to reach them is called:
Nemawashi
Catchball
Gemba walk
X-matrix

Catchball passes objectives and means up and down the organization until each level commits to what it can deliver. Nemawashi is informal consensus building before a decision, not the structured negotiation of targets in hoshin planning.

A strategic objective is to cut warranty costs 30%. How should the quality manager deploy quality methods to support it?
Charter projects on the top warranty failure modes
Raise final inspection sampling on all products
Launch a company-wide quality awareness campaign
Ask design engineering to review all warranty claims

Pareto analysis of warranty data points improvement projects, each with an owner and measure, at the failure modes that drive most of the cost. Heavier final inspection adds appraisal cost and does not remove the causes of field failures.

At a mid-year hoshin review, one annual objective has been red for three months. What is the appropriate response?
Analyze the gap and adjust the means via PDCA
Lower the target to match recent performance
Assign a new owner who will push the team harder
Hold the decision until the year-end review
Hoshin reviews treat a red objective as a problem to study: find why the means are not working and change them, applying PDCA. Lowering the target hides the gap instead of learning from it.

A quality manager delegates building the annual supplier audit schedule to a senior engineer. What should the manager hand over with the task?
Authority that matches the responsibility assigned
Final accountability for how the schedule turns out
A step-by-step method the engineer must follow
A rule that each added supplier needs her sign-off

Delegation works only when the person gets the authority to make the decisions the task requires. Accountability for the outcome stays with the manager who delegated, and prescribing the method or approving every step is micromanagement, not delegation.

III.A.1
A plant set a monthly scrap standard of 2%, and this month scrap was 3.5%. As part of the controlling function, what should the plant manager do next?
Raise the standard to 3.5% so it matches the results
Reassign the scrap metric to a different department
Wait for a second month of data before looking at it
Find why performance deviated and act to correct it

Controlling means setting standards, measuring, comparing results with the standard and taking corrective action on the gap. Moving the standard to fit one bad month removes the signal instead of acting on it.

III.A.1

A quality manager has two auditors this month. Requests are a customer-required process audit due in two weeks, a routine internal audit with no open findings, and an audit of a supplier whose rejects tripled last quarter. How should she allocate the auditors?
Split their time equally across all three so each request gets attention
Do the routine internal audit first because it is already on the schedule
Cover the customer and supplier audits first and reschedule the routine one
Ask for a third auditor and hold all three audits until one is hired

Resources should go where risk and commitments are greatest: the customer deadline and the supplier with tripled rejects. The routine audit, with no open findings, can safely move. Splitting time equally treats unequal risks as if they were equal, and waiting for new staff leaves the urgent work undone.

A supervisor times each motion of an assembly task, specifies the one best method and pays a bonus for output achieved with that method. Which theory is she applying?
Human relations theory
Scientific management
Systems thinking
Contingency theory

Taylor’s scientific management studies work methods, standardizes the best one and links pay to output. Human relations theory, which grew out of the Hawthorne studies, focuses on social and motivational factors rather than task engineering.

A manager gives close direction to a new hire but lets a veteran team set its own methods within agreed goals. Which approach does this reflect?
Autocratic style
Contingency approach
Transactional style
Scientific management
The contingency (situational) approach holds that no single style fits every case; the manager adjusts to the people and the task. An autocratic manager would direct both groups closely.

A department head mainly sets targets, rewards people who meet them and steps in when results fall short. Which management style is this?
Transactional
Transformational
Participative
Coaching

Transactional management is an exchange of rewards for agreed performance, with correction when targets are missed. Transformational leadership instead inspires people around a shared vision and develops them to go beyond set targets.

III.A.2
In a tense project review, a manager notices her frustration rising, pauses, and acknowledges the team’s concerns before responding. Which concept does this show most directly?
Management by fact
Scientific management
Transactional management
Emotional intelligence

Recognizing and managing one’s own emotions and reading others’ are core parts of emotional intelligence. Management by fact concerns basing decisions on data, which is not what the manager is doing in this moment.

A sales manager promises a major customer a two-week lead time without checking with production or purchasing. What is the most likely result?
Higher satisfaction because the quoted lead time is shorter
Lower inventory because material is ordered only on demand
Missed dates or costly expediting
Better forecasts because sales took ownership of the order

A delivery promise depends on production capacity and material availability that sales does not control. The faster quote may please the customer at first, but missed dates or expediting costs follow when other functions were not part of the commitment.

Purchasing wants to switch to a cheaper resin supplier to meet its cost target. Which function most needs to be involved before the change is made?
Marketing, to decide how to announce the change to buyers
Finance, to book the savings in this year’s budget
Engineering, to confirm the resin meets design requirements
Human resources, to update the purchasing job descriptions

Each department is measured only on its own metrics, and improvements in one department often hurt another. What is the underlying problem?
Departments have too few people to meet all their goals
Measures ignore how departments depend on one another
Targets were set too low to drive real improvement
Metrics are reviewed too rarely by senior management

When each function optimizes its own numbers without regard to the process it shares with others, the system suboptimizes. Adding staff or reviewing more often does not fix measures that reward one function at another’s expense.

III.A.4
Only one technician can program the coordinate measuring machine, and he plans to retire in 18 months. What should the quality manager do?
Cross-train a successor now and document his methods before he leaves
Hire a replacement after he leaves and the role is open
Offer a retention bonus so he delays his retirement
Stop CMM inspection and rely on hand gages instead

Succession planning prepares people for critical roles before they are vacant, and documented methods capture what the incumbent knows. A retention bonus only postpones the same gap, and hiring after he leaves loses the chance for him to train someone.

Which individual objective best supports a department’s quality goals?
Show stronger commitment to quality in every task this year
Attend all scheduled quality meetings during the year
Support the quality policy in daily work at all times
Cut rework on line 3 from 4% to 2% by the end of the second quarter
A useful objective is specific, measurable and time-bound and ties to a department result. The others describe activity or attitude that cannot be measured against an outcome.

A suggestion program recognizes only the single best idea each quarter, and participation has fallen. Which change is most likely to restore it?
Raise the value of the quarterly prize for the single top idea
Make one suggestion per quarter mandatory for all staff
Move the award to an annual event with a larger audience
Recognize every implemented idea promptly, in proportion to its value

Frequent, timely recognition tied to contribution tells everyone their ideas count. A bigger single prize still leaves almost everyone unrecognized, and mandatory suggestions produce volume, not engagement.

Which financial statement shows a company’s assets, liabilities and owners’ equity at a single point in time?
Income statement
Cash flow statement
Balance sheet
Operating budget
The balance sheet is a snapshot of financial position on one date. The income statement, the most common confusion, reports revenue and expenses over a period.

III.A.5
A $100,000 test station will save $40,000 a year for three years with no salvage value. At a 10% discount rate, what does net present value show?
About +$20,000, so it clearly meets the 10% hurdle
About −$526, so it does not meet the 10% hurdle
About +$99,474, so it easily meets the 10% hurdle
About +$8,000, so it comfortably meets the 10% hurdle

The present value of $40,000 a year for three years at 10% is about $99,474, so NPV is about −$526. The +$20,000 figure ignores the time value of money by simply adding the cash flows, and +$99,474 is the present value of the savings before subtracting the investment.

A quality manager proposes a $40,000 vision system that will save $50,000 in its first year. What is the first-year return on investment?
ROI is net gain divided by cost: ($50,000 − $40,000) / $40,000 = 25%. The 125% figure is savings divided by cost, a benefit-cost ratio, which does not subtract the investment.

III.A.5
Project A pays back its cost in 1.5 years and then ends. Project B pays back in 2.5 years but keeps saving for eight years. Choosing A on payback alone ignores what?
Cash flows that arrive after the payback point
The initial investment that each project requires
The speed at which each project recovers its cost
The savings each project earns during its first year

Payback measures only how quickly the investment is recovered, so it ignores everything earned afterward and also ignores the time value of money. Speed of recovery is exactly what payback does measure, so it is not the blind spot.

What does ISO 9001:2015 require of an organization regarding risk?
Keep a documented FMEA for every process in the management system
Adopt the full ISO 31000 risk management framework
Eliminate every identified risk before production starts
Determine risks and opportunities and plan proportionate actions

ISO 9001:2015 requires risk-based thinking: identify risks and opportunities and act in proportion to their potential impact on conformity. It does not mandate FMEA, a formal ISO 31000 framework or the elimination of all risk.

A manufacturer buys cargo insurance to cover losses from damaged export shipments. Which risk treatment is this?
Avoiding the risk
Retaining the risk
Sharing the risk
Reducing the likelihood
Insurance moves part of the financial consequence to another party, which is sharing or transferring the risk. It does not make damage less likely, as better packaging would.

A new regulation will ban a chemical used in the plating line two years from now. What is the best risk-based response?
Wait until the ban takes effect and then find a substitute
Assess the impact now and qualify a substitute early
Stockpile enough of the chemical to cover the next five years
Ask the customer to waive the requirement for the plated parts

A known regulatory change is a risk to plan for early, because qualifying a new chemistry takes time. Stockpiling would not keep the plant compliant once the ban applies, and waiting turns a manageable change into a crisis.

Ask him to write a detailed procedure covering everything he knows
Pair newer operators with him for structured mentoring on the job
Record his settings in the maintenance database for reference
Send newer operators to a classroom course on press theory

Project teams record lessons learned at closure, yet the same problems recur on later projects. What is the most likely gap?
Lessons are filed but not used to update standards or plans
Teams record lessons too late in the project to be accurate
Too few people attend the lessons learned meetings
The lessons learned template has too few categories

Capturing lessons has value only when they change standards, checklists or the planning of new projects. Better timing or attendance would improve the record but would not stop recurrence if nobody applies it.

III.A.7
Engineers keep know-how to themselves because promotions reward individual expertise. Which action best addresses this barrier?
Buy a knowledge management platform for the engineers
Issue a policy that requires engineers to share know-how
Limit access to technical files to senior engineers only
Recognize knowledge sharing in evaluations and promotions

The barrier is the incentive, so the fix is to reward sharing. A new platform does not change why engineers hold back, and a policy mandate without changed incentives tends to produce minimal compliance.

III.B.1
A quality manager must tell a production supervisor that his area received a major finding in a customer audit. Which approach is best?
Send a detailed email so he has the finding in writing
Announce the finding at the next all-hands meeting
Meet face to face, then follow up with a written summary
Post the audit report on the area’s communication board

Sensitive news calls for a rich, two-way channel where reactions and questions can be handled, with writing to confirm details. An email alone gives the facts but not the chance to discuss them, and a public announcement embarrasses the supervisor.

III.B.1
An engineer’s report to executives is full of statistical terms and gets no response. What should she change first?
Add more statistical detail to prove that the analysis is rigorous
Send the same report again with a higher priority flag
State the findings in terms of cost, risk and the decision needed
Shorten the report by cutting the data and conclusions
The barrier is a message not adapted to its audience. Executives act on cost, risk and clear choices; more statistics would widen the gap, and cutting the conclusions removes what they need to act.
std
III.B.1
On a video call, a supervisor says he agrees with a new inspection plan, but he looks away and sits with his arms crossed. What should the manager do?
Accept his verbal agreement and assign him the first action item
Ask open questions to draw out any concerns he has not voiced
Tell him his body language shows that he disagrees
End the call and send the plan to him in an email

Nonverbal cues that conflict with words are a reason to check understanding, not to conclude. Open questions invite concerns safely; telling him what his posture means is a judgment that may be wrong and puts him on the defensive.

III.B.2
An inspector explains that the new shift schedule leaves too little time for end-of-shift checks. Which response shows active listening?
“So there isn’t time to finish checks before handoff?”
“I know exactly how you feel; I had the same issue once.”
“Have you tried starting the checks earlier in the shift?”
“Let’s set this aside until the schedule settles down.”
Paraphrasing the speaker’s point confirms understanding and shows attention. Jumping to a suggestion may be well meant, but it skips confirming what the problem actually is.

III.B.2
A supplier’s account manager calls, angry that a lot was rejected. What should the quality manager do first?
Restate the rejection decision firmly and end the call
Escalate the call to the supplier’s general manager
Offer to accept the lot under deviation to calm him
Acknowledge his concern and review the evidence together
Acknowledging emotion lowers tension, and reviewing the objective evidence keeps the conversation on facts. Accepting the lot to end the conflict trades product quality for comfort.

III.B.2
Two engineers argue in a meeting, each blaming the other for a failed trial. How should the manager respond?
Decide which engineer is right and close the topic as quickly as possible
Ask both engineers to drop the issue to keep the peace
Assign the follow-up to whoever has the most seniority
Separate the facts from the opinions and focus on the problem
Objectivity means steering the discussion away from blame and toward the evidence about the trial. Asking them to drop it avoids the conflict but leaves the cause of the failure unknown.

III.B.3
A team spans South Carolina, Monterrey and Shanghai, and the weekly call is always at 9 a.m. Eastern. What is the best fix?
Keep the time fixed so everyone knows when to expect the call
Hold separate calls at each site and skip the joint meeting
Rotate meeting times and post written updates
Ask the Shanghai members to send a delegate to the US site

Rotating times shares the burden fairly, and asynchronous updates keep people informed when they cannot attend. A fixed 9 a.m. Eastern slot is predictable, but it lands at 9 or 10 p.m. in Shanghai, so the same members always carry the inconvenience.

III.B.3
A US engineer writes an expiry date of 03/04/2027 on a label for a European site. What is the risk, and the fix?
None, since the date format is set by the standard for labels
It may read as 3 April; use 2027-03-04
It may be read as 2003; write the year with four digits first
It may be read as a lot number; add the words “expiry date”
Many countries write day before month, so 03/04 is read as 3 April instead of March 4. An ISO 8601 date or a spelled-out month removes the ambiguity.

III.B.3
Translated work instructions are causing assembly errors at a site abroad. Which safeguard is most effective?
Back-translate them and verify them with local users
Use the original English instructions at that site
Add a glossary of English terms at the end of each one
Run the text through a second translation software tool

Back-translation into the source language exposes changes in meaning, and checking with the people who use the instructions confirms they are understood. Another software pass may repeat the same errors with no human check.

III.B.4
A customer complaint email thread has 30 recipients, including the customer. An engineer wants to discuss internally which department caused the problem. What should he do?
Start a separate thread with only the internal people involved
Reply all so the customer sees the issue is being worked
Reply all but mark the message as internal in the subject
Forward the thread to his manager and copy the customer

III.B.4
A newly formed virtual team across three sites keeps missing handoffs. What should the team leader do first?
Require every member to join a daily two-hour video meeting
Ask each site to follow its own preferred tools and habits
Replace email with instant messaging for all team traffic
Agree team norms for channels, response times and decisions
Virtual teams need explicit agreements on which channel to use for what, how fast to respond and where decisions live. Long daily meetings add load without fixing the handoff rules.

III.B.4
Since a department moved most updates to chat, misunderstandings on complex design issues have grown. What should the manager do?
Ban chat and move all communication back to formal memos
Ask people to write longer chat messages with more detail
Use richer media such as calls for complex topics
Require a read receipt on every chat message about design
Complex or ambiguous topics need richer, two-way media where questions can be answered at once. Longer chat messages are still one-way and slow to resolve misunderstanding.

III.C.1
Before approving a new improvement project, what should the sponsor confirm first?
The team members have open time on their calendars
It supports a strategic objective with a clear business case
A detailed Gantt chart has already been prepared
The project leader has run a similar project before

III.C.1
Formally accepting deliverables, releasing resources and recording lessons learned take place in which phase?
Execution
Closure
Monitoring and controlling
Planning
Closure confirms the deliverables are accepted, releases the team and captures lessons. Monitoring and controlling tracks performance during the project but does not end it.
std
III.C.1
A team will build a software tool for audit scheduling, but users cannot yet say exactly what they need. Which approach fits best?
Iterative, delivering working pieces in short cycles for feedback
Linear, fixing all requirements up front before any build
Linear, with a detailed design approved before user contact
Iterative, but with user review held back until the final release
When requirements are uncertain, short iterations with user feedback let the requirements emerge and keep rework small. A linear approach depends on stable requirements that this team does not have.
std
III.C.2
Task A (3 days) starts the project. Task B (4 days) and Task C (6 days) both follow A, and Task D (2 days) follows both B and C. How many days can B slip without delaying the project?
0 days
4 days
11 days
2 days
Path A–C–D takes 11 days and A–B–D takes 9, so the critical path is A–C–D and B has 11 − 9 = 2 days of float. Zero float applies only to tasks on the critical path.
std
III.C.2
For a task, the optimistic estimate is 4 days, the most likely is 7 and the pessimistic is 16. What is the PERT expected time?
9 days
7 days
8 days
10 days
PERT expected time is (O + 4M + P) / 6 = (4 + 28 + 16) / 6 = 8 days. A simple average of the three estimates gives 9 days, which ignores the extra weight PERT gives the most likely value.
std
III.C.2
A project manager needs to break the deliverables into work packages small enough to assign and estimate. Which tool should she use?
Gantt chart
PERT estimate
Work breakdown structure
Risk assessment matrix

A WBS decomposes the project scope into deliverables and work packages, which then become the basis for cost and time estimates. A Gantt chart schedules tasks over time but assumes they have already been defined.
std
III.C.2
On a 1–5 risk matrix, Risk X has likelihood 4 and severity 2, Risk Y has likelihood 2 and severity 5, and Risk Z has likelihood 3 and severity 3. Which risk should get attention first?
Risk X
Risk Y
Risk Z
All three equally
Multiplying likelihood by severity gives X = 8, Y = 10 and Z = 9, and Y also carries the highest severity. X is the most likely, but likelihood alone ignores the size of the consequence.
std
III.C.3
At a status review, the work completed is worth $50,000 of budget, the planned value to date is $60,000, and actual cost is $55,000. What is the cost variance?
−$5,000, meaning the work done cost more than budgeted
−$10,000, meaning the work done cost more than budgeted
+$5,000, meaning the work done cost less than budgeted
−$15,000, meaning the work done cost more than budgeted
Cost variance is earned value minus actual cost: $50,000 − $55,000 = −$5,000. The −$10,000 figure is the schedule variance (earned value minus planned value), which measures progress, not cost.
std
III.C.3
Midway through a project, actual spending is 30% below the planned budget. What should the project manager conclude?
The project is running efficiently and is comfortably under budget
The budget was set too high and should be cut by 30%
The savings can be moved to other projects right away
Nothing yet; check whether the work is also behind schedule

Comparing spend with the plan alone cannot tell good efficiency from work that simply has not been done. Underspending is often a sign of delay, so progress must be checked before calling it a saving.
std
III.C.3
A milestone on the critical path, design freeze, has slipped three weeks. What should the project manager do?
Keep the end date and expect later tasks to absorb the delay
Report the slip at the final project review once it is known
Remove the milestone from the plan so the report stays green
Assess the end-date impact and agree recovery with the sponsor

A critical path slip moves the end date unless work is recovered, so the impact has to be assessed and a decision made with the sponsor now. Hoping later tasks absorb it ignores that critical path tasks have no float.
std
III.C.4
An improvement project changed how a heat-treat process is run. What must happen before the team hands the process back to its owner?
Write the change into the team’s final presentation slides
Email the operators a summary of the new process settings
Update the controlled procedure and train the people who use it
Leave the old procedure in place until the next annual review
Gains hold only when the new method is in the controlled documents people work from and they are trained on it. Slides and emails are not controlled and are easy to lose or ignore.
std
III.C.4
At closure, a sponsor disputes whether a deliverable was in scope. The change was agreed verbally months ago. What practice would have prevented this?
A larger budget reserve set aside for unplanned scope additions
A change log of each approved change and who approved it
More frequent team meetings to discuss the state of the scope
A longer charter that tries to list every possible deliverable
Written, approved records of scope changes give an agreed baseline at closure. Meetings and longer charters do not create a record of what was decided after the project started.
std
III.C.4
What should a project summary report contain so others can use it later?
Objectives against results, key decisions, lessons and open items
A full copy of every email and meeting note from the whole project
Each team member’s hours charged to the project by week
The project schedule with no comments on how it was met

A summary should let a reader understand what was intended, what was achieved, why key choices were made and what remains. Raw email archives and timesheets bury that information rather than summarize it.
std
III.D.1
Which element must a quality policy include under ISO 9001:2015?
A commitment to continual improvement of the QMS
Numeric targets for scrap, returns and complaints
A list of the procedures that make up the QMS
The names of the managers responsible for quality

ISO 9001 requires the policy to commit to meeting applicable requirements and to continual improvement, and to provide a framework for objectives. Numeric targets belong in the quality objectives, not the policy itself.
std
III.D.1

A company’s mission stresses fast delivery of custom-engineered equipment. The draft quality policy says the company will deliver only standard catalog designs with zero deviation. What should the quality manager do?
Approve the policy, since standard designs reduce defects
Ask leadership to change the mission to match the policy
Publish both and let each department pick which to follow
Revise the policy so that it also supports quality in custom work

The quality policy must be consistent with the organization’s purpose and strategic direction. Standard designs may reduce defects, but a policy that contradicts the mission will either be ignored or work against the business.
std
III.D.1
How can the quality manager best judge whether the quality policy is actually deployed?
Check that every employee can recite the policy word for word on request
Count the posters showing the policy in each work area
Check that objectives trace to it and staff can explain their part
Confirm that all managers have signed the policy statement
Deployment shows when objectives link to the policy and people understand how their work contributes. Reciting the words shows memorization, not understanding or alignment.
std
III.D.2
A new contract carries special inspection and traceability requirements beyond the plant’s normal practice. What should the quality manager prepare?
A full rewrite of the quality manual to add the new requirements
A contract quality plan naming the processes, controls and owners for the order
A memo to supervisors asking them to take extra care on the job
A new company-wide procedure that applies the rules to all orders

A quality plan states which processes, resources, controls and responsibilities apply to a specific product or contract. Rewriting the manual or imposing the rules on all orders adds cost where the requirements do not apply.
std
III.D.2
Procedures are kept current on a shared drive, but operators work from printed copies of outdated revisions. What should be fixed?
More frequent revisions of the procedures on the shared drive
Current copies at every point of use, with obsolete ones removed
A rule that operators must memorize the current procedures
A yearly reminder email listing the latest revision numbers

Controlled documents must be available where they are used, and obsolete copies must be withdrawn or clearly marked. Revising the master more often makes the problem worse if the floor copies still lag.
std
III.D.2
Top management set annual quality objectives, but most supervisors cannot say what they are. What is the best next step?
Cascade the objectives to each function with owners, actions and measures
Repeat the objectives at the next all-employee town hall meeting and in newsletters
Add the objectives to the quality manual for future reference
Ask supervisors to sign a form confirming they read them

Deployment means translating top-level objectives into actions and measures each function owns. Repeating or filing the objectives raises awareness at most; it does not give supervisors anything to act on.
std
III.D.3
Customer complaints fell 40% this year, but warranty returns rose. What should the quality manager conclude?
The quality system is improving, as shown by fewer complaints
Warranty data are less reliable than complaint data and can wait
The complaint process is working and needs no further review
Complaints alone understate dissatisfaction; analyze the returns
Many dissatisfied customers never complain, so complaint counts can fall while problems grow. Rising returns are direct evidence of field failures and need analysis.
std
III.D.3
Which of these is a required input to management review under ISO 9001:2015?
Salary data for the quality department staff
Detailed production schedules for each shift
Results of internal and external audits
Individual appraisal ratings of each auditor

ISO 9001 lists audit results among the required inputs, along with customer satisfaction, process performance, nonconformities and supplier performance. Personnel salary and appraisal data are not QMS performance inputs.
std
III.D.3
A mock recall takes three days to trace a lot of finished goods to the customers who received it, and the target is four hours. What does this show?
The recall plan works, since every customer was eventually found
The four-hour target is unrealistic and should be relaxed
The traceability system is not effective and must be improved
Traceability is a logistics matter outside the quality system
A mock recall tests whether the system can act in time to protect customers. Finding everyone eventually is not enough when a real recall needs fast containment.
std
III.E.1
An organization wants a third-party certificate for its quality management system. To which standard is it certified?
ISO 9000
ISO 9001
ISO 9004

ISO 9001 contains the requirements an organization can be certified against. ISO 9000 gives the fundamentals and vocabulary, ISO 9004 is guidance for sustained success, and ISO 19011 is guidance for auditing.
std
III.E.1
A plant manager insists that decisions be based on the analysis of data and information. Which ISO 9000 quality management principle is this?
Evidence-based decision making
Process approach
Improvement
Relationship management

Evidence-based decision making holds that decisions based on analysis of data are more likely to produce intended results. The process approach is about managing activities as interrelated processes, not about how decisions are made.
std
III.E.1
A contract manufacturer builds only to customer designs and does no design work. How should it handle the ISO 9001 design and development clause?
Write a design procedure anyway so the system is fully complete
Ask the customer to perform design reviews on its behalf
Exclude the clause without giving any justification at all
Declare it not applicable, with justification

ISO 9001 lets an organization state that a requirement does not apply if it justifies this and the exclusion does not affect product conformity. A procedure for work the company never does adds paperwork without value.
std
III.E.1
An auditor writes a nonconformity against ISO 9001:2015 because a company has no quality manual. Is the finding valid?
Yes, a quality manual is a required document in every edition
Yes, unless the company has fewer than 50 employees
No, because documented information is no longer required
No, the 2015 edition does not require a quality manual

ISO 9001:2015 dropped the requirement for a quality manual, though the organization must keep the documented information the standard and its own system require. Saying that documented information is no longer required overreaches: the 2015 edition replaced “documents and records” with “documented information” but did not remove the requirement.
std
III.E.2
A team visits a best-in-class plant to learn its changeover methods before measuring its own changeovers. What is the problem?
It should have visited a direct competitor instead of a best-in-class plant
It should have sent a written survey rather than visiting
Without a baseline it cannot size the gap or know what to adopt
It should have waited for the leader to publish its methods

Benchmarking starts by understanding and measuring one’s own process, so the comparison shows the size of the gap and which practices matter. The choice of partner or data collection method does not fix a missing baseline.
std
III.E.2
A company compares on-time delivery and practices across its own five plants to spread the best methods. What type of benchmarking is this?
Competitive
Internal
Generic
Functional
Internal benchmarking compares units within the same organization, where data are easy to get. Competitive benchmarking compares against direct competitors, which these plants are not.
std
III.E.2
What most distinguishes total quality management from a stand-alone continuous improvement program?
TQM is an organization-wide approach that involves everyone
TQM is a certifiable standard with defined requirements
TQM relies mainly on final inspection to catch defects
TQM uses only large breakthrough projects led by experts

TQM is a management philosophy that integrates customer focus, involvement of all employees and continuous improvement across the whole organization. Continuous improvement is one element within it. TQM is not a certifiable standard; ISO 9001 is.
std
III.E.3
A quality director organizes the department’s work around quality planning, quality control and quality improvement. Whose framework is this?
Juran
Crosby
Ishikawa
Shewhart
The quality trilogy of planning, control and improvement is Juran’s. Crosby’s approach centers on zero defects and the price of nonconformance.
std
III.E.3
A manager sets zero defects as the performance standard and measures quality as the price of nonconformance. Whose ideas is he applying?
Deming
Feigenbaum
Juran
Crosby

Zero defects as the performance standard and quality measured by the price of nonconformance are central to Crosby’s approach. Deming opposed slogans and targets such as zero defects that do not give workers a method to achieve them.
std
III.E.3
A supervisor disciplines the operators with the highest daily defect counts, although the process is in statistical control. How would Deming view this?
Discipline is right because it holds each operator personally accountable
Discipline is right if it is applied fairly to every operator
The variation comes from the system, which management must change
Discipline is wrong only because defect counts are too small

Deming held that most variation belongs to the system, which only management can change, so ranking and blaming workers for common cause variation is unfair and ineffective. Applying discipline fairly does not fix the error of blaming people for the system.
std
III.E.3
Which quality leader introduced total quality control and described the “hidden plant,” the capacity lost to rework and fixing errors?
Ishikawa
Feigenbaum
Shewhart
Deming

Feigenbaum coined total quality control and the hidden plant. Ishikawa promoted company-wide quality control and quality circles in Japan, which is easy to confuse with Feigenbaum’s total quality control.
std
IV.A.1
A team has agreed on its problem statement and now wants to sort the many possible causes members suggest into groups such as methods, machines, materials and people. Which tool fits?
Fishbone diagram
Stratified check sheet
Frequency histogram
Cross-functional flowchart

A fishbone (cause and effect) diagram organizes suspected causes under category headings so none are overlooked. A check sheet is tempting because it also uses categories, but it records how often things happen rather than structuring possible causes.
std
IV.A.1
A histogram of shaft diameters from one product line shows two distinct peaks. What is the most likely explanation?
The process is stable and centered between the specification limits
Output from two different sources, such as two machines, is mixed
The gauge resolution is too coarse to separate nearby values
The process mean is drifting slowly in one direction over time

A bimodal histogram usually means two populations with different centers have been combined, so the data should be stratified by machine, shift or material. Coarse gauge resolution produces a comb-like or gapped histogram, not two separate humps.
std
IV.A.1
A scatter diagram shows a strong positive relationship between oven temperature and coating hardness. A manager wants to raise the temperature to its maximum at once. What is the soundest response?
Raise the temperature now, since the diagram proves it drives hardness
Ignore the diagram, because scatter plots cannot show relationships
Confirm cause and effect with a controlled trial before acting
Wait until the correlation coefficient reaches exactly 1.0 before acting

Correlation shows the two variables move together but does not prove that one causes the other; a lurking variable could drive both, and the relationship may not hold outside the observed range. Acting immediately treats correlation as proof of causation.
std
IV.A.1
A Pareto analysis of 100 defects shows scratches 45, dents 25, misalignment 15, discoloration 10 and other 5. What share of all defects do the top two categories account for?
45 percent
85 percent
25 percent
70 percent
Scratches and dents total 45 + 25 = 70 of 100 defects, or 70 percent. 85 percent is the cumulative share of the top three categories, a common misread of the cumulative line.
std
IV.A.2
After customer interviews, a team has written about 90 comments on sticky notes and wants to sort them into natural groupings without forcing preset categories. Which tool fits?
Affinity diagram
Interrelationship digraph
Tree diagram
