Activity network diagram

An affinity diagram groups many ideas or verbal data by their natural similarity, usually silently, and then names the groups. An interrelationship digraph comes later, to map cause and effect between a smaller set of issues that are already defined.
std
IV.A.2
In an interrelationship digraph, one issue has many outgoing arrows and almost no incoming arrows. How should the team treat it?
As a key outcome to use as a measure
As a likely root driver to address first
As an isolated issue that can be set aside
As the lowest-priority issue in the set

Outgoing arrows show what an issue influences, so an issue with many outgoing arrows drives the others and is a candidate root cause. An issue with many incoming arrows is the opposite: a key outcome that is useful as an indicator but not a lever.
std
IV.A.2
A project manager is planning an ERP rollout and wants to list, for each step, what could go wrong and the countermeasure to prepare in advance. Which tool fits?
Affinity diagram
Prioritization matrix
Process decision program chart
Matrix diagram

A PDPC extends a plan or tree diagram by asking what could go wrong at each step and recording countermeasures. A matrix diagram shows relationships between two or more sets of items but does not lay out contingencies along a plan.
std
IV.A.2

A prioritization matrix weights cost at 0.4 and impact at 0.6, scored 1 to 5 (higher is better). Proposal W scores cost 5, impact 2; X scores 2, 5; Y scores 4, 4; Z scores 3, 3. Which proposal ranks first?
Proposal X, with a weighted score of 3.8
Proposal W, with a weighted score of 3.2
Proposal Z, with a weighted score of 3.0
Proposal Y, with a weighted score of 4.0

Weighted scores are W 0.4(5) + 0.6(2) = 3.2, X 3.8, Y 1.6 + 2.4 = 4.0 and Z 3.0, so Y ranks first. X is tempting because it has the highest score on the heaviest criterion, but its weak cost score pulls it below Y.
std
IV.A.3
A defect appears on line 2 but not on lines 1 and 3, began in March, and occurs only on nights. Which tool is built to use contrasts like these to narrow the search for the cause?
Is/is-not analysis
Failure mode and effects analysis
A3 report
PDCA cycle

Is/is-not analysis compares where, when and how much the problem occurs with where it could occur but does not; the differences point to what changed. An A3 report is a format for telling the whole problem-solving story, not a technique for isolating the cause.
std
IV.A.3
A customer finds defective parts on its assembly line. Under the 8D method, after the team is formed and the problem is described, what comes next?
Identify and verify the root cause of the defect
Implement and verify interim containment actions
Choose and verify permanent corrective actions
Recognize the team's work and close the report

8D puts containment (D3) right after team formation and problem description so the customer is protected while the cause is found. Root cause analysis is D4; doing it before containment leaves defective parts flowing in the meantime.
std
IV.A.3

In an FMEA, failure mode X has severity 9, occurrence 2 and detection 2 (RPN 36); failure mode Y has severity 4, occurrence 5 and detection 5 (RPN 100). The team plans to act only on Y. What is the main concern?
Y's RPN is too low to justify any action from the team
The RPNs were multiplied when they should have been added
X may need action because its severity is so high
Detection ratings should not be part of the risk ranking

RPN multiplies severity, occurrence and detection, so a low occurrence or good detection can hide a severe effect. High-severity modes generally warrant review regardless of RPN, which is why newer FMEA guidance favors action priority over a pure RPN ranking.
std
IV.A.3
An auditor finds a mislabeled bin. The supervisor relabels it and closes the finding the same day. In ISO 9000 terms, what has been done?
A corrective action
A preventive action
A root cause analysis
A correction only

Relabeling eliminates the detected nonconformity, which ISO 9000 calls a correction. Corrective action would also find and remove the cause, such as why the labeling process allowed the error, so the finding should not yet be closed as corrected.
std
IV.A.4
During a brainstorming session, a senior engineer critiques each idea as it is offered and contributions are drying up. What should the facilitator do?
Remind the group that judgment waits until idea generation ends
Have the engineer rank ideas as they come in to save time later
Hold a vote after each idea so that weak ideas drop out early
Let the most experienced members speak first to set direction

Brainstorming separates generating ideas from evaluating them; criticism during generation suppresses quantity and unusual ideas. Ranking or voting on each idea as it arrives brings the evaluation back into the generation phase.
std
IV.A.4
A 5 whys analysis of a pump failure ends at “the operator forgot to lubricate the bearing.” What is the main weakness?
It asked too many whys and went beyond the useful cause
It blames a person, not the process that allowed it
It should have started from a fishbone diagram instead
It needs a Pareto chart before the result can be accepted

Stopping at human error usually leads to retraining or blame, and the miss recurs. Asking why the process allowed lubrication to be skipped (no schedule, no indicator, no checklist) reaches a cause the organization can fix.
std
IV.A.4
A company is designing a new product line for which no process yet exists and wants to build in quality from the start. Which approach fits?
DMAIC, because it is the standard six sigma roadmap
Statistical process control on the new line's output
Design for six sigma, using a roadmap such as DMADV
Kaizen events on the closest existing product line

DFSS roadmaps such as DMADV design a new product or process to meet customer requirements at high capability. DMAIC improves an existing process with a measurable baseline, which a line that does not yet exist cannot provide.
std
IV.A.5
Which of these is a prevention cost?
Calibrating final inspection gauges
Scrapping parts that fail in-process test
Processing customer warranty returns
Training operators in a new work method

Training is spent before production to stop defects being made, so it is prevention. Calibrating inspection gauges is tempting because it seems preventive, but it supports evaluating product and is an appraisal cost.
std
IV.A.5
A plant's annual cost of quality is prevention $20,000, appraisal $50,000, internal failure $80,000 and external failure $150,000. What percent of total cost of quality is failure cost?
About 77 percent
About 50 percent
About 27 percent
About 23 percent
Failure cost is 80,000 + 150,000 = 230,000 of a 300,000 total, about 77 percent. 50 percent counts external failure alone, and 23 percent is prevention plus appraisal.
std
IV.A.5
A company substantially increases its spending on prevention, such as design reviews and supplier development. What is the expected pattern over time?
Total cost of quality rises by the new spending
Failure costs fall and total cost of quality drops
Appraisal costs must rise to verify the new work
Internal failure rises while external failure falls

Effective prevention stops defects from being made, so internal and external failure fall, appraisal can often be reduced, and total COQ declines. Internal failure rising while external falls is the signature of added inspection, not added prevention.
std
IV.A.5
A plant adds 100 percent final inspection without changing the process. What is the most likely short-term effect on cost of quality?
Prevention cost rises because inspection is a prevention activity
Internal and external failure costs both fall right away
Internal failure rises as escapes are caught in the plant instead
Total cost of quality falls because fewer defects are made

Inspection is appraisal; it catches defects already made, moving them from external to internal failure while appraisal cost climbs. The defect rate itself is unchanged, so failure costs do not both fall and total COQ usually rises.
std
IV.B.1
A process owner is setting a first-pass yield goal for a new packaging line. What should the goal be based on?
The best yield any single shift has reached on the line last month
The highest yield published in the industry, applied as is
The figure operators think they can reach with no changes
Customer needs and the strategy, checked against the line's demonstrated capability

Goals should flow from what customers and the strategy need and be tested against what the process can do, so the gap tells management what improvement is required. A one-shift best or an industry figure ignores both the customer and the line's actual capability.
std
IV.B.1
An on-time delivery goal of 95 percent has been met for six months, yet customer complaints about late deliveries are rising. What should the quality manager do first?
Check whether the metric's definition matches the customer's
Raise the goal to 98 percent so the process keeps improving
Treat the complaints as noise, since the goal is being met
Add a second shipping shift to increase delivery capacity

When a goal is met but customers are unhappy, the measure is suspect: it may count against a revised promise date or ship date rather than the date customers asked for. Raising the target on a flawed measure only tightens the wrong thing.
std
IV.B.1
A call center sets a goal that every call be handled in under three minutes. Within weeks, average handle time drops but repeat calls rise sharply. What best explains this?
Customers have started calling more often for unrelated reasons
The goal drives agents to end calls before issues are resolved
The three-minute goal was not strict enough to change behavior
Repeat calls show that agents need more product training

A numerical target without a method, and without balancing measures, invites people to hit the number at the expense of the outcome, as Deming warned. More training might help resolution, but it does not explain why repeat calls rose at the same moment the goal took effect.
std
IV.B.2
A four-step process has one resource per step with cycle times of 3, 5, 4 and 2 minutes per unit. What is the maximum throughput?
30 units per hour
20 units per hour
12 units per hour
4.3 units per hour

Throughput is set by the slowest step, 5 minutes, so 60 / 5 = 12 units per hour. 4.3 units per hour comes from dividing by the summed cycle time, which is lead time for one unit, not the rate of a flowing process.
std
IV.B.2
An order-handling process holds an average of 120 orders in progress and completes 40 orders per day. What is the average time an order spends in the process?
0.33 days
80 days
160 days
3 days
Little's law gives lead time = work in process / throughput = 120 / 40 = 3 days. 0.33 days results from inverting the ratio.
std
IV.B.2
A process review finds operators follow a sequence different from the written work instruction, and their method gives better yield. What should the analyst recommend?
Verify the operators' method, then revise the instruction to match it
Retrain operators to follow the written instruction exactly as issued
Raise a nonconformance against each operator who deviated
Leave both as they are, since the current yield is acceptable

Documents should describe the best known method; once the better method is confirmed with data, the instruction should be updated so everyone uses it. Retraining to the old instruction would lower yield, and leaving the gap means new staff learn the worse method.
std
IV.B.3
A machine has availability of 90 percent, performance of 80 percent and quality rate of 95 percent. What is its OEE?
88.3 percent
68.4 percent
72.0 percent
95.0 percent
OEE multiplies the three factors: 0.90 x 0.80 x 0.95 = 0.684. 88.3 percent is their average, which overstates OEE because each loss compounds the others.
std
IV.B.3
A team observing a two-hour changeover is starting a SMED effort. What should it do first?
Buy faster tooling for the machine's die change
Increase batch sizes to spread the setup cost
Separate internal setup tasks from external ones
Move all changeovers to the end of each shift

SMED begins by sorting tasks into internal (machine stopped) and external (can be done while running), then moving as many as possible to external. Larger batches hide the long setup and add inventory instead of shortening it.
std
IV.B.3
A supermarket of parts sits between two cells, and the upstream cell builds only when a card comes back from the downstream cell. What does this arrangement achieve?
Upstream builds to a forecast set at the start of the week
The downstream cell can draw on unlimited buffer stock
Each cell keeps its own utilization as high as possible
Upstream output is triggered only by actual downstream consumption

This is a kanban pull system: a returned card is the signal to replace what was consumed, which caps inventory and links production to real demand. Building to forecast is push scheduling, the approach kanban replaces.
std
IV.B.3
An assembly fixture is redesigned so that a part physically cannot be loaded backward. Which lean tool is this?
Poka-yoke
Kanban
Standard work
5S

A device that makes an error impossible or immediately obvious is poka-yoke (mistake-proofing). Standard work defines the correct sequence, but it relies on people following it rather than preventing the wrong action.
std
IV.B.4
A plant improves the efficiency of an operation that is not its constraint. What is the expected effect on plant throughput?
A rise in proportion to the operation's efficiency gain
Little or none, while inventory ahead of the constraint grows
A rise only if operating expense also goes up
A fall, because the constraint loses its protective buffer

In TOC the system is a chain whose output is limited by its weakest link, so a local gain at a non-constraint leaves system throughput unchanged and may only pile up work in front of the constraint. Assuming a proportional rise is the local-optimum thinking TOC warns against.
std
IV.B.4

All machines in a plant have idle capacity, material is available and orders are waiting, yet shipments are late because a rule requires a batch of 500 before any release. What type of constraint is this?
A physical constraint
A market constraint
A policy constraint
A material constraint

A rule, measure or practice that limits throughput is a policy constraint, and it can often be removed at little cost. It is not physical because no machine is short of capacity, and not a market constraint because demand exceeds output.
std
IV.B.4
In Goldratt's theory of constraints, which describes operating expense?
Money generated through sales less variable costs
Money invested in things the system intends to sell
Labor cost charged only to the constraint resource
Money spent turning inventory into throughput

Goldratt defines operating expense as all the money the system spends to turn inventory into throughput. Money generated through sales less truly variable costs is throughput, and money invested in things the system intends to sell is inventory.
std
IV.C.1
A newly formed team wants to measure every variable it can find on a process, but data collection time is limited. What should guide what it measures?
The few variables linked to the project's critical outputs
Whatever the existing systems already record automatically
Every variable, so that nothing is missed in the analysis
The variables that are least expensive to collect by hand

Measurement should be driven by the question being answered: the outputs that matter to the customer and the inputs suspected of driving them. Collecting only what is already recorded is cheap, but it may omit the variables that matter.
std
IV.C.1
Two inspectors on the same shift report very different scratch counts for the same lot of parts. What should be done before more data are collected?
Average the two inspectors' counts to get a fair figure for the lot
Write an operational definition, with examples, of a scratch
Keep only the higher count as the safer estimate for the customer
Increase the sample size so that differences average out

Inconsistent counts usually mean the inspectors judge the same thing differently; an operational definition with boundary samples makes the measurement repeatable. A larger sample does not fix a definition problem, since the bias between inspectors remains.
std
IV.C.1
A team can record each part's measured diameter or simply pass or fail. Why is the measured value often worth its higher cost per reading?
It needs no gauge study because measuring instruments are objective
It allows control limits to be set equal to the specification limits
It carries more information, so smaller samples can detect changes
It removes the need to define when and where samples are taken

Variable data show how far and in which direction parts vary, so shifts can be seen with far fewer readings than pass/fail data require. Measured values still depend on the gauge, so a measurement system analysis is still needed.
std
IV.C.2
A company's customers are 70 percent small accounts and 30 percent large accounts, whose needs differ. Survey results must represent both groups reliably. Which sampling approach fits?
Simple random sampling
Convenience sampling
Sampling only large accounts
Stratified random sampling

Stratified sampling divides the population into groups that differ and samples randomly within each, so both are represented with known precision. A simple random sample may by chance include too few of one group to draw conclusions about it.
std
IV.C.2
What defines a simple random sample?
Every possible sample of that size has an equal chance of being picked
Units are chosen at a fixed interval from a list
Units are drawn from each subgroup in proportion
Units are those easiest for the inspector to reach

In a simple random sample every possible sample of the chosen size, and therefore every unit, has the same chance of selection. Picking at a fixed interval is systematic sampling, which can be biased if the list has a repeating pattern, and drawing from each subgroup in proportion is stratified sampling.
std
IV.C.2
In which situation is sampling, rather than 100 percent inspection, clearly the right choice?
Brake components on every aircraft built
Weld pull tests that destroy the part
A run of five custom assemblies
An in-line gauge already checks each part

When a test destroys the item, inspecting everything would leave nothing to ship, so sampling is the only option. Safety-critical aircraft brakes are the opposite case, where the consequence of a missed defect justifies checking every unit.
std
IV.C.3
Five measurements are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 10. What are the mean and median?
Mean 4, median 5
Mean 5, median 5
Mean 5, median 4
Mean 4, median 4
The mean is 25 / 5 = 5, and the median is the middle value of the ordered data, 4. The single high value of 10 pulls the mean above the median.
std
IV.C.3
Five measurements are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 10. What is the sample standard deviation?

Squared deviations from the mean of 5 total 9 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 25 = 36; dividing by n - 1 = 4 gives a variance of 9, and the square root is 3.0. Dividing by n instead gives about 2.7, the population formula, and 9.0 is the variance itself.
std
IV.C.3
Order processing times are skewed to the right, with a few orders taking far longer than most. Which statement is correct?
The mean is higher than the median
The median is higher than the mean
The mean, median and mode are equal
The mode is higher than the mean

The long right tail pulls the mean toward the high values while the median stays with the typical order, so the mean exceeds the median. Mean, median and mode coincide only in a symmetric distribution such as the normal.
std
IV.C.3
An X-bar and R chart shows all points within control limits with no patterns, yet about 5 percent of product is out of specification. What should the manager conclude?
A special cause is present and should be found and removed now
The process is stable but not capable; the system itself must change
The control limits are wrong and should be reset to the specification
The process is capable because it is in statistical control

Stability means the variation is predictable; it says nothing about whether that variation fits within the specification. Searching for a special cause wastes effort, because the defects come from common-cause variation or centering that only a change to the process will fix.
std
IV.C.4
A gauge R&R study shows reproducibility is much larger than repeatability. Where should improvement focus?
On the gauge itself, such as wear, fixturing or resolution
On the parts, by choosing samples with less part-to-part variation
On how the appraisers use the gauge, such as method and training
On the specification, by widening the tolerance the parts must meet

Reproducibility is variation between appraisers measuring the same parts, so a large value points to differences in technique, setup or interpretation. Wear and resolution problems in the gauge show up as poor repeatability, the variation within one appraiser's repeated readings.
std
IV.C.4
Repeated readings of a reference standard are tightly clustered but average 0.05 mm above its known value. How is this measurement system best described?
Accurate but imprecise
Accurate and precise
Imprecise and unbiased
Precise but biased

Tight clustering means good precision, while a consistent offset from the reference value is bias, so the system is not accurate. Precision and bias are separate properties, and a gauge can be strong on one and weak on the other.
std
IV.C.4
A gauge reads correctly near the bottom of its range but increasingly high toward the top of its range. This is a problem of:
Linearity
Stability
Repeatability
Reproducibility

Linearity is a change in bias across the operating range of the gauge. Stability is a change in bias over time, which would show up as drift on repeated checks of the same reference rather than a pattern across the range.
std
IV.C.5
Customer calls about a beverage product peak every July and dip every January, year after year. This is best described as:
An upward trend
A seasonal pattern
A process shift
A random pattern
A rise and fall tied to the same calendar period each year is seasonal. A trend is a sustained movement in one direction, which this data does not show over the years.
std
IV.C.5
On an X-bar chart, the subgroup averages rise steadily over many consecutive subgroups, all still within the control limits. What is the most likely cause?
A one-time change of material lot
Mixing two machines in each subgroup
A gradual drift, such as tool wear
Common-cause variation alone

A steady run upward signals a cause that builds over time, such as tool wear or temperature creep, even before any point crosses a limit. A one-time change of lot would show a step to a new level, not a steady climb.
std
IV.C.5
After a new resin supplier started, the last nine points on an individuals chart all sit above the center line, with none beyond the limits. What is the right interpretation?
No signal exists, because no point is beyond the control limits
The control limits are too wide and should be tightened at once
Gradual tool wear is the likely cause of the pattern on the chart
A likely shift in the process mean, worth investigating

A long run on one side of the center line is very unlikely under common-cause variation alone, so it signals a shift; its timing points to the new resin. Treating only points beyond the limits as signals ignores the run rules that detect sustained shifts.
std
IV.C.6
A stable process is in control, but a supervisor adjusts the machine after every reading above or below target. What is the likely effect?
Variation increases, because common-cause noise is treated as signal
Variation decreases, because each error is corrected as it appears
The process mean shifts away from target, but variation stays the same
There is no effect, because each adjustment cancels the previous one

Adjusting a stable process in response to common-cause variation is tampering; as Deming's funnel experiment shows, it adds the adjustment error to the natural variation. Variation would fall only if the readings reflected real special causes.
std
IV.C.6
A single point falls far above the upper control limit on the day of a power interruption. What is the appropriate response?
Recalculate the limits so that the point falls inside them
Investigate that point's circumstances and act on the cause
Redesign the whole process to reduce overall variation
Ignore it, because a single point is not a real pattern

A point beyond a control limit is a special-cause signal; it should be investigated and the cause removed or guarded against. Redesigning the process is the response to excessive common-cause variation, not to an isolated event.
std
IV.C.6
A process is in statistical control, but its variation is too large to meet customer needs. Who is best placed to reduce the variation?
Operators, by adjusting after high readings
Inspectors, by tightening the sort criteria
Management, by changing the system
Suppliers, by adding conformance certificates

Common-cause variation comes from the system itself, its methods, equipment, materials and design, which management controls, so only a change to the system reduces it. Operator adjustments to a stable process are tampering and add variation.
std
IV.C.7
A characteristic has specification limits of 4 and 16. The process mean is 13 and the standard deviation is 1. What are Cp and Cpk?
Cp = (16 - 4) / (6 x 1) = 2.0. Cpk takes the nearer limit: (16 - 13) / (3 x 1) = 1.0. Cpk can never exceed Cp, which rules out the 1.0/2.0 and 2.0/3.0 options.
std
IV.C.7
A process has Cp of 1.8 but Cpk of 0.9. What does this tell the quality manager?
The spread fits the tolerance, but the process is off center
The spread is too wide for the tolerance, but it is centered
The process is out of statistical control and unpredictable
The measurement system cannot detect the process variation

Cp compares the spread with the tolerance and ignores location, while Cpk includes the distance to the nearer limit; a large gap between them means the process is not centered. Recentering would raise Cpk toward Cp without reducing variation.
std
IV.C.7
For a process, Ppk is much lower than Cpk. What does this most likely indicate?
The sample used for Ppk was too small to be of any use
Shifts or drift between subgroups add to the variation within them
The process is better centered over the long run than short
The specification limits were changed between the studies

Cpk uses within-subgroup variation, while Ppk uses the overall variation of all data, which also includes movement between subgroups over time. A large gap means the process is not stable, so long-term performance is worse than its short-term potential.
std
IV.C.8
A new electronic product shows a high failure rate in its first weeks of use that then falls to a low, steady level. Which phase is this, and what is a common response?
Wear-out; scheduled replacement before the end of life
Useful life; no action since failures are random
Infant mortality; burn-in or screening to remove weak units
Wear-out; extending the warranty period to cover it

A decreasing early failure rate is the infant mortality region of the bathtub curve, caused by latent manufacturing or component defects, and burn-in screens them out. Wear-out is the rising failure rate at the end of life, not the start.
std
IV.C.8
Maintenance introduces quick-change modules that cut average repair time from four hours to one hour. Which measure improves directly?
Mean time between failures
Infant mortality rate
Failure rate in useful life
Mean time to repair
MTTR measures how long it takes to restore an item after a failure, so faster repair lowers it directly. MTBF measures how often failures occur, which faster repair does not change.
std
IV.C.8
Before a new filling line is released, the team tests the equipment across its specified operating ranges to show it performs as intended. This activity is:
Operational qualification
Installation qualification
Performance qualification
Burn-in testing

Operational qualification shows the equipment operates as intended throughout its specified operating ranges. Installation qualification only confirms it was installed correctly, and performance qualification then shows the process consistently makes conforming product under normal conditions.
std
V.A.1
The shipping department keeps receiving incomplete order paperwork from order entry, and customer shipments go out late as a result. What should the quality manager do first?
Have shipping and order entry agree on what a complete order packet must contain
Add a paperwork check at the shipping dock before each order is released
Send late customers a letter explaining the internal paperwork delays
Warn order entry clerks that incomplete forms will go on their reviews

Shipping is order entry's internal customer, so the fix is to define that customer's requirements at the source. A dock check only catches bad packets after the delay has already started, and blaming clerks ignores that the requirement was never made explicit.
std
V.A.1
Which of the following is an internal customer?
An employee who buys the company's products at the staff discount price
A department that uses another department's output to do its own work
A distributor that resells the organization's finished products
An outside contractor who performs work on the company's site
An internal customer is defined by receiving work output inside the organization, not by being an employee. An employee buying product at a discount is acting as an external customer of that product.
std
V.A.1
Six months ago, maintenance and production signed an internal service agreement to cut equipment downtime. How should the quality manager judge whether it worked?
Count how many agreement review meetings the maintenance supervisors attended
Survey maintenance technicians on whether they like the new agreement
Compare downtime and on-time delivery to external customers before and after
Confirm the agreement was signed and filed by both department managers

The point of improving an internal customer relationship is the effect on process results and, through them, on external customers. Meeting attendance, staff opinion and signatures are activity measures that say nothing about outcomes.
std
V.A.2
A medical device maker is developing a new infusion pump for hospitals. Which approach most directly brings external customer requirements into the design?
Have engineering derive requirements from the current pump's drawings
Ask the sales team to estimate which features competitors will offer next
Release the pump and gather feature requests from early field complaints
Involve clinicians in setting requirements and testing prototypes

Users who will operate the device are the source of its requirements, and involving them early lets the design reflect real use. Copying the old design or guessing competitor moves leaves customer needs untested, and waiting for complaints finds gaps after release.
std
V.A.2
For a contract manufacturer that builds products for brand owners, which of these is an external customer?
The consumer who buys the finished product in a store
The assembly line that receives machined parts from the machine shop
The purchasing team that selects the plant's raw material suppliers
The plant's quality lab that tests incoming material samples

External customers sit outside the organization and include end users further down the chain, not just the direct buyer. The assembly line, purchasing and the lab all receive work inside the plant, so they are internal customers.
std
V.A.2
A key customer repeatedly changes specifications after orders are released, and the supplier scraps material each time. Which strategy best addresses this?
Refuse every specification change once the customer has placed an order
Hold joint requirement reviews with the customer before each order is released
Absorb the changes and raise prices across all customers to cover scrap
Build extra stock to the old specification in case the change is reversed

Working with the customer to settle requirements earlier attacks the cause and keeps the relationship. A blanket refusal damages the relationship, spreading the cost penalizes other customers, and extra stock to an old revision adds waste.
std
V.A.3

A distributor serves 2,000 small shops and 40 national chains. The chains want electronic ordering and a dedicated account manager; the small shops want low minimum orders and quick phone help. What does segmentation suggest?
Give every account the service level the national chains want
Run all accounts through one standard process to keep costs low
Design a separate service and delivery model for each group
Drop the small shops so resources can go to the national chains

Segmentation exists so service and delivery can match what each group values. Serving everyone at chain level overspends on shops that do not value it, and one standard process fits neither group well.
std
V.A.3
A software firm groups its customers by how often they log in and which features they use. This is segmentation by:
Demographics
Geography
Psychographics
Behavior

Grouping by usage patterns is behavioral segmentation. Psychographic segmentation uses attitudes, values and lifestyle, which is the most likely confusion, while demographic and geographic segmentation use who and where customers are.
std
V.A.3

A company segments customers by industry, but complaint data show that across every industry, satisfaction depends mainly on whether customers need technical support. What should the quality manager recommend?
Rebuild the segments around support needs, which drive satisfaction
Keep the industry segments because they match the sales organization
Increase technical support by the same amount for every customer
Combine all customers into a single segment to simplify reporting

Segments are useful only if they separate customers whose needs differ; the data show support need is the real dividing line. Keeping segments for internal convenience ignores the evidence, and adding support for everyone spends money where it is not valued.
std
V.A.4
Which of the following is subjective information?
The number of days between order receipt and product delivery
A focus group member's remark that the packaging “feels cheap”
The percentage of orders shipped complete in the last quarter
The measured force in newtons required to open the sealed package
A verbatim focus group comment records a perception in the customer's words. The other three are objective measures that anyone using the same method would record the same way.
std
V.A.4
A hotel chain collects hundreds of open-ended guest comments each month and wants to track how complaints change over time. What should it do with the comments?
Have each manager read the comments and judge the overall trend by feel
Replace the comment box with a single 1 to 10 overall rating question
Code them into defined categories and count each category every month
Track the average length of the comments as an indicator of satisfaction

Coding verbatim comments into categories turns them into counts that can be trended while keeping their meaning. Reading by feel is inconsistent across managers, and a single rating loses the detail about what went wrong.
std
V.A.4
A survey asks customers to rate “ease of use” from 1 to 5, and the company also measures how long customers take to finish a set task. How does the rating differ from the time measure?
It is objective because the customer's answer is recorded as a whole number
It should be discarded because perceptions cannot be measured at all
It is more reliable because it comes straight from the customers
It records perception and is best read alongside the objective time data

A rating scale captures the customer's perception; recording it as a number does not make it objective. Perception matters, so it should be kept and interpreted together with objective measures rather than dropped or ranked above them.
std
V.B.1
In a quality function deployment house of quality, the rows on the left (the “whats”) list:
Customer requirements
Technical characteristics
Competitor benchmark ratings
Target values for the design
The house of quality starts from the voice of the customer, listed as the whats. Technical characteristics are the hows across the top, and targets and benchmarks sit in other rooms of the house.
std
V.B.1
In a house of quality, what does the triangular “roof” show?
How important each customer requirement is relative to the others
Whether technical characteristics support or conflict with one another
How customers rate the product against each major competitor
How strongly each technical characteristic meets each customer requirement

The roof is the correlation matrix among the hows, which exposes design trade-offs. The strength of each how against each what is recorded in the central relationship matrix, which is the most common confusion.
std
V.B.1

A QFD team rates customer needs A, B and C at importance 5, 3 and 2. Technical characteristic X relates strongly (9) to A and weakly (1) to B. Characteristic Y relates moderately (3) to A, strongly (9) to B and strongly (9) to C. What are the technical importance scores of X and Y?

Technical importance is the sum of importance times relationship: X = 5x9 + 3x1 = 48 and Y = 5x3 + 3x9 + 2x9 = 60, so Y ranks higher. Summing the relationship weights alone gives 10 and 21, looking only at need A gives 45 and 15, and leaving out need C gives 42 for Y.
std
V.B.1
A feature that delighted customers five years ago is now offered by every competitor, and customers expect it. How should the product team treat it in planning the next model?
As a delighter that still sets the product apart from competitors
As an optional premium feature that customers will pay extra for
As a low priority, since customers have stopped asking for it
As a basic requirement whose absence would cause dissatisfaction

Under the Kano model, delighters drift into expected, basic requirements over time. Customers stop mentioning basic needs precisely because they assume them, so dropping it or treating it as a differentiator would be a mistake.
std
V.B.2
Each of three customers buys $40,000 a year at a 25% gross margin, and each would be expected to stay another 5 years. If all three are lost now, about how much margin is lost over that period?

Margin per customer per year is $40,000 x 0.25 = $10,000, so 3 customers x 5 years gives $150,000. $600,000 uses revenue instead of margin, $30,000 counts only one year, and $50,000 counts only one customer.
std
V.B.2
A retention program costs $20,000 a year and is expected to keep 4 customers who would otherwise leave, each worth $8,000 a year in profit. What is the program's net annual benefit?
Retained profit is 4 x $8,000 = $32,000, less the $20,000 program cost, for a net $12,000. $32,000 ignores the cost and $52,000 adds it instead of subtracting it.
std
V.B.2
A company's complaint rate is low and has fallen for three quarters. Why should the quality manager not conclude that customers are satisfied?
Complaint data are confidential and so cannot be used for any trend analysis
Complaints track service problems rather than product quality problems
Many unhappy customers leave without complaining, so complaints undercount them
A low rate shows that customers have no remaining concerns that they care about

Complaints are one listening post and capture only the customers who choose to speak up; many dissatisfied customers simply defect. Surveys, warranty data, interviews and retention figures are needed to see the rest.
std
V.B.2
Survey satisfaction scores are high, yet the share of customers who renew each year is falling. What should the quality manager do first?
Raise the target satisfaction score for next year's survey
Survey the currently satisfied customers more frequently each year
Offer every customer a loyalty discount at the next renewal
Interview customers who did not renew to learn why they left

Satisfaction does not guarantee loyalty, and the customers who left hold the information the survey is missing. Surveying the remaining customers more often repeats the blind spot, and a blanket discount acts before the cause is known.
std
V.B.3
Customers calling a support line complain that they must explain their problem to three different agents before it is fixed. Which change best supports good customer service?
Give first-contact agents the tools and authority to solve common issues
Script a courteous greeting for agents to use after every call transfer
Add more transfer options to the automated phone menu for callers
Set a target to cut the average length of each call by one minute

The failure is in rapid response and easy access: the customer cannot reach someone able to help. A polite greeting does not remove the transfers, and a call-length target can push agents to transfer even more.
std
V.B.3
An upset customer calls about a late order. Which agent response best demonstrates active listening?
Reading the delivery policy so the customer understands the terms
Restating the problem and confirming it before proposing a fix
Explaining at once that the freight carrier caused the late delivery
Promising a refund before learning what the customer needs

Active listening means showing the customer they have been understood, and restating and confirming does that. Quoting policy or blaming the carrier centers the company, and a premature refund may not be what the customer wants.
std
V.B.3
A service manager wants a measure that shows how well the team meets the principle of rapid response. Which measure fits best?
Number of calls each agent handles in a single eight-hour shift
Percentage of calls opened with the approved greeting
Time from a customer's first contact to a useful reply
Total number of customer contacts received each month
Rapid response is about how quickly the customer gets help, so it is measured from the customer's side. Calls per agent is a productivity measure that can rise while customers wait longer.
std
V.B.4
A plant is at full capacity when two major customers each ask for their orders to be expedited. What should the operations and quality managers do?
Serve whichever customer calls and escalates the issue most often
Split the capacity evenly between them regardless of contract terms
Promise both customers their requested dates and catch up with overtime later
Apply the agreed priority rules and give each customer a realistic date

Conflicting demands are handled by priorities set in advance, applied consistently and communicated honestly. Rewarding whoever escalates is arbitrary, and promising dates the plant cannot meet damages trust with both customers.
std
V.B.4
A service firm's workload from several clients peaks on different days of the week. Which approach best manages capacity across these clients?
Forecast demand by client and staff each day to the combined load
Staff every day of the week to cover the highest single-day peak
Give each client a fixed team that does not change with volume
Accept all requests and work through the backlog in order

Because the peaks fall on different days, combining the forecasts lets staffing follow the real total load. Staffing every day for the peak wastes capacity, and fixed teams leave some idle while others are overloaded.
std
V.B.4
A bank is expanding to serve customers who speak several languages and include many older adults. What is the main implication for product and service design?
A design built for the largest group will serve the other groups just as well
Access, communication and usability needs must be gathered from each group
Diverse groups matter to marketing campaigns but not to process design
Translating the current materials is all that the bank needs to change

Diverse customer groups can differ in every aspect of how they use a service, so their requirements must be captured directly. Translation addresses language only and misses needs such as accessibility for older adults.
std
VI.A
A company needs a new supplier for a safety-critical machined part. What should happen before production orders are released?
Approve the supplier once it signs the purchase terms and quality clauses on the order
Assess its process and inspect a first article of the part before approving it
Release the first order to the lowest bidder and inspect the parts after they arrive
Approve the supplier based on references from two other customers in the industry

For a safety-critical part, approval should rest on evidence that the supplier can make this part: an assessment of its process and a first article inspection. Signed terms set obligations but show nothing about capability.
std
VI.A
A buyer says a candidate supplier’s ISO 9001 certificate proves its parts will meet the company’s drawings. What is the most accurate response?
The certificate proves the supplier’s processes are capable for every part it produces
It shows a conforming quality system, not that this part will meet requirements
The certificate means the supplier’s parts can be exempted from incoming inspection
The certificate is of little value, so the supplier should be judged on price alone

An ISO 9001 certificate says a registrar found the quality management system conforming to the standard; it does not verify capability for a particular product or specification. It is a useful input to selection, not proof of product conformity.
std
VI.A
A company has 600 suppliers and limited audit resources. What is the most effective way to set the level of oversight each supplier receives?
Audit every supplier on the same annual schedule regardless of what it supplies
Classify suppliers by how critical their output is and how they perform, and match controls
Audit the suppliers with the largest annual spend and exempt all of the smaller ones
Rotate audits alphabetically so that every supplier is visited every few years

Risk-based classification puts the most control where a supplier’s output has the greatest potential effect on the product and where performance is weakest, as ISO 9001 expects. Spend is a poor proxy: a low-cost part can be safety critical.
std
VI.A
Candidate suppliers are rated 0–100 on quality (weight 50%), delivery (30%) and cost (20%). X scores 95, 70, 70; Y scores 75, 90, 100; Z scores 90, 85, 80. Which supplier ranks highest?
Supplier Y, with an average score of 88.3
Supplier X, with the top quality score of 95
Supplier Y, with a weighted score of 84.5
Supplier Z, with a weighted score of 86.5
Weighted scores are X 82.5, Y 84.5 and Z 86.5 (for Z: 0.5×90 + 0.3×85 + 0.2×80). Y has the highest unweighted average, which is the tempting mistake, but the agreed weights put quality first.
std
VI.B
A critical component comes from a single supplier whose only plant sits in a flood-prone region. What is the most appropriate risk response?
Increase incoming inspection on the component to catch any flood-related defects
Qualify a second source or hold buffer stock to cover the recovery time
Add a contract clause that obliges the supplier to guarantee uninterrupted supply
Accept the risk because the supplier’s quality record has been excellent to date

The risk is loss of supply, so the response must reduce the likelihood or the impact of an interruption: a second source or a buffer covering recovery time. A contract clause shifts blame but cannot deliver parts the supplier cannot make.
std
VI.B
A supplier review looks only at on-time delivery and PPM. Which risk is it most likely to miss?
Shipments that arrive after the delivery date agreed on the order
Defective parts that reach the company’s receiving dock
Financial weakness that could end the supplier’s operations
Defective parts that operators find during final assembly

Delivery and PPM metrics show quality and timeliness after the fact; they do not reveal the supplier’s financial health, which can fail with little warning. A broader risk assessment adds financial, capacity, geographic and sub-tier factors.
std
VI.B
A tier-1 supplier is well managed but buys a key chip from a single sub-tier source. What should the buying company’s supplier risk assessment do?
Map the critical sub-tier sources and include them in the risk assessment
Leave sub-tier risk to the tier-1 supplier, since it holds that contract
Audit every sub-tier supplier in the whole chain once a year without exception
Move the component to a different tier-1 supplier as soon as possible

A disruption at a single sub-tier source stops the buyer’s line just as surely as one at tier 1, so critical sub-tier dependencies belong in the assessment. The tier-1 supplier manages its own sources, but the risk to the buyer remains the buyer’s to understand.
std
VI.B
An offshore supplier quotes a unit price 20% below the domestic incumbent. Before switching, what should the quality manager insist on?
A total cost comparison covering lead time, inventory, freight and quality
Confirmation that the offshore unit price will stay fixed for the first year
Proof that the offshore supplier holds a current ISO 9001 certificate
Agreement from finance that the saving meets this year’s cost target

Unit price is only part of the cost: longer lead times raise inventory and expose the line to longer recovery from quality problems. A total cost of ownership view shows whether the saving survives. A certificate says nothing about these costs.
std
VI.C

A supplier ships parts that meet every drawing dimension, but the finish on a sealing surface varies widely because the supplier checks it rarely. The drawing gives a finish callout but does not flag it. What would most likely have prevented this?
Tightening the tolerances on all of the dimensions shown on the drawing
Marking the finish as a critical characteristic on the drawing and PO
Holding supplier review meetings more often throughout the year
Requiring the supplier to inspect every dimension on every part shipped

Suppliers set their controls by what they know matters. Identifying the sealing finish as critical makes the expectation explicit so the supplier controls and verifies it. Tighter dimensional tolerances do nothing for an unflagged finish.
std
VI.C
A supplier finds that a lot it has already shipped may contain parts with the wrong heat treatment. What should the supplier quality agreement require?
Correction of its own process first, then notice to the customer to avoid causing alarm
A report on the issue at the next scheduled quarterly business review meeting
Prompt notice to the customer through the agreed escalation route, naming the lots
A credit note for the affected lot if the customer later finds the defect itself

Suspect product already in the customer’s hands needs immediate containment, so the agreement should require prompt notice through a defined emergency channel. Fixing the process first delays the customer’s containment while the parts move toward use.
std
VI.C
What is the main purpose of regularly scheduled performance review meetings with key suppliers?
Renegotiate the unit price at every meeting using the latest quality figures
Replace formal nonconformance reports with quicker verbal status updates
Let the supplier request relaxed requirements where it is struggling to comply
Review performance data together and agree on actions before problems escalate
Routine reviews give both sides a shared view of the data and a set time to agree on actions while issues are still small. They add to formal nonconformance reporting; they do not replace it.
std
VI.D
In one quarter a supplier delivered 40,000 parts, of which 60 were rejected as nonconforming. What is its defect rate in parts per million?
150 PPM
667 PPM
PPM = 60 ÷ 40,000 × 1,000,000 = 1,500. The rate is 0.15%, and reading 0.15% as 150 PPM or 15,000 PPM is the usual decimal-place slip.
std
VI.D
A supplier has a 50 PPM defect rate and is rated “preferred,” yet the plant keeps stopping for its late shipments. What does this show about the rating system?
It rates quality alone and needs delivery and service measures as well
Its PPM target is too loose and should be lowered closer to zero
The plant should carry more safety stock instead of changing the rating
Late shipments are a logistics issue outside supplier quality management

Supplier performance covers quality, cost, delivery and service. A rating built on PPM alone can call a supplier preferred while it disrupts production. Tightening the PPM target only sharpens the measure that is already being met.
std
VI.D
Which metric best measures a supplier’s responsiveness?
Percentage of lots accepted at incoming inspection over the quarter
Percentage of orders received by the date requested on the order
Change in unit price compared with the same quarter of last year
Average time from a nonconformance notice to an accepted containment plan

Responsiveness is how quickly the supplier acts when asked, so time from notice to containment measures it directly. Lot acceptance measures quality, on-time receipt measures delivery and price change measures cost.
std
VI.D
A sole-source supplier has failed repeatedly despite several corrective action cycles, and it holds tooling owned by the company. What is the soundest exit approach?
Qualify an alternate source first, then plan the transfer of tooling and stock
End the purchase agreement at once to send the supplier an unmistakable warning
Keep the supplier and add permanent 100% inspection of its parts at receiving
Ask the supplier to certify conformance on each shipment and leave it in place

An exit from a sole source must protect continuity: a qualified alternate, a build-ahead or bridge plan and recovery of owned tooling and inventory come first. Ending the agreement at once leaves the company with no parts and its tooling in a dispute.
std
VI.E
Defects from one supplier have risen on one part family while its other parts are fine. Which audit is most likely to find the cause?
A system audit of the supplier’s entire quality management system
A product audit of finished parts held in the supplier’s warehouse
A process audit of the operations that make the affected part family
A financial audit of the supplier’s cost structure and profit margins

A process audit examines how the operations that make the affected parts are run and controlled, which is where the cause is likely to be. A product audit confirms whether finished parts conform but does not show why they fail.
std
VI.E
A supplier’s corrective action report gives the root cause as “operator error” and the action as “operator retrained.” What should the supplier quality engineer do?
Accept it, because retraining the operator addresses the root cause that was stated
Accept it once the operator has signed a training record covering the procedure
Reject it and require the supplier to remove the operator from the job permanently
Reject it and ask why the process allowed the error and what will stop a repeat

“Operator error” rarely is a root cause; the analysis should ask why the process let the error happen and change the process, for example with error-proofing. Retraining alone seldom prevents recurrence.
std
VI.E
A supplier reports that its corrective action for a recurring dimensional defect is in place. What should happen before the action is closed?
Close it when the supplier submits its signed corrective action report
Close it once the supplier’s next audit score shows an improvement
Verify the action works using data from the lots that follow
Close it after the supplier’s quality manager confirms it in writing
Closure needs evidence that the problem has stopped, such as several subsequent lots free of the defect. A signed report shows the action was taken, not that it worked.
std
VI.E
A small but capable supplier of a hard-to-replace part keeps struggling to run SPC on a critical characteristic. What is the most effective response?
Help it build the skill through joint training and on-site support
Issue a formal warning letter and cut its share of future business awards
Raise the incoming inspection sampling level until its SPC results improve
Add a contract penalty for every out-of-control point on its SPC charts

When a supplier is worth keeping and the gap is a skill, supplier development fixes the cause at the source. Warnings and penalties add pressure without adding the know-how, and more inspection only sorts the output.
std
VI.F
A company wants to certify suppliers so their parts can go to stock without incoming inspection. What should certification require?
Capability data, a sustained record of good lots and an on-site process review at its plant
A current third-party ISO 9001 certificate and a signed supplier quality agreement
A long purchasing history and the lowest total cost within its commodity group
A successful first article inspection on each part number it currently supplies

Removing incoming inspection is safe only when evidence shows the supplier’s processes will keep producing good parts: capability data, a sustained performance record and an on-site process review. An ISO 9001 certificate and a quality agreement do not show part-level capability.
std
VI.F
A certified supplier’s defect rate has risen for two quarters in a row. What should the certification program do?
Leave its status unchanged until its certification comes up for renewal next year
Reassess its status under the program’s rules and restore inspection if needed
Remove it from the approved supplier list at once and begin resourcing its parts
Take no action until a customer complaint can be traced back to the supplier

Certification is earned and kept on performance, so the program should define what triggers a review and how status is reduced. Restoring inspection protects the product while the supplier recovers; dropping the supplier at once is out of proportion to a trend.
std
VI.F
A company wants to move a key supplier from arm’s-length bidding to a partnership. Which change best reflects that move?
Share forecasts and design plans, and set joint goals under a multiyear agreement
Rebid the work every year so the supplier keeps its prices at market levels
Shift all inspection to the supplier without changing anything else about the relationship
Add a financial penalty clause for every late or defective shipment it sends
Partnerships rest on long-term commitment, shared information and joint goals, so both sides invest in improvement. Annual rebidding and penalty clauses are the tools of an arm’s-length relationship.
std
VI.G
Under a ship-to-stock arrangement, purchased parts:
Are inspected 100% at receiving before being placed in stock
Stay at the supplier’s site until the customer calls them off
Ship only when a kanban signal is sent from the production line
Go straight to stores or the line without incoming inspection

Ship-to-stock means the supplier’s demonstrated performance lets parts bypass receiving inspection. Shipping on a kanban signal describes a pull or JIT trigger, not the inspection status of the parts.
std
VI.G
A plant moves a component to just-in-time delivery in small daily lots. What is the main implication for supplier quality?
Incoming inspection must sample each of the small lots more heavily than before
Quality matters less, because small lots limit how many defects can arrive
Defects stop the line quickly, so quality must be built in at the supplier's source
The supplier should hold extra safety stock to replace any rejected lots

JIT removes the inventory that once hid defects, so a bad lot halts production almost at once. That calls for capable, controlled supplier processes, not more receiving inspection, which adds delay that JIT is meant to remove.
std
VI.G
Incoming inspection uses a sampling plan with an AQL of 1.0%, and a lot is accepted. What can the receiving manager conclude?
The lot as a whole contains no more than 1.0% defective units
Every unit in the lot conforms to the purchase order specification
The sample passed, but the lot may still contain some defective units
The supplier’s process capability index for the part is at least 1.0

Acceptance sampling judges the lot from a sample, so an accepted lot can still contain defectives, and the AQL is not a guarantee about any single lot’s quality. The OC curve shows the chance of accepting lots at each defect level.
std
VII.A
A company’s strategic plan calls for entering the medical device market in two years. How should the training manager build next year’s training plan?
Repeat last year’s plan, adjusted for the courses with the highest reaction scores
Derive the competencies the strategy needs, such as ISO 13485, and close the gaps
Let each department choose courses from the catalog up to its own budget limit
Wait until the first medical contract is signed before planning any training

A training plan aligned to strategy starts from the capabilities the strategy requires, such as medical device quality system requirements, and closes the gap ahead of need. Popular courses and departmental choice do not ensure that alignment.
std
VII.A
Two plant managers will retire in three years and no internal candidate is ready to replace them. What belongs in the training plan?
A general leadership course offered to every employee across the company
A plan to recruit external replacements once the managers set their dates
Advanced technical courses for the two plant managers before they retire
Development plans for likely successors, with mentoring and job rotations

Succession needs targeted leadership development for named candidates, combining experience, mentoring and formal training over the time available. A company-wide course spreads effort thin and does not prepare anyone specific.
std
VII.A
An engineer’s personal development plan includes a course in a field the business has no need for. What should her manager do?
Approve it as written, since development plans belong to the employee alone
Remove the course and assign training chosen solely by the department instead
Defer all of her development activity until her next promotion review
Discuss how her goals fit business needs and agree on a plan serving both

Personal development plans work best when individual aspirations and business needs are aligned through discussion. Approving it unchanged ignores the business; imposing courses undermines the engagement the plan is meant to build.
std
VII.A
Which of these belongs in a training plan rather than in the training materials?
The step-by-step exercise the learners will complete during class
The slides and handouts used to explain each learning objective
Who will be trained, by when, by which delivery method and at what total cost
The answer key for the knowledge test at the end of the course
A training plan sets out the who, what, when, how and cost of training so it can be resourced and tracked. Exercises, slides and test answers are part of the materials that deliver the content.
std
VII.A
Training for a new ERP system was delivered on schedule, two weeks before the planned go-live, but go-live has now slipped by four months. What is the main risk to the training plan?
Trainees will gain extra time to master the system well before go-live
The training budget will need to double to cover the four-month delay
The trainers will need to be recertified on the system before go-live
Trainees will forget much of what they learned before they can use it

People lose skills they do not use soon after learning them, which is why training is timed just before it is needed. Without access to the live system, the four months give trainees time to forget rather than master it, so the plan needs refresher training scheduled close to the new go-live date.
std
VII.B
Order-entry errors have risen and a manager asks for retraining. What should the training analyst do first?
Schedule refresher training this month for every person who works in order entry
Survey the order-entry staff on which training topics they would most prefer
Find out whether a skill gap or something else, such as workload, is the cause
Add a knowledge test on order entry to the next round of performance reviews

Training fixes only knowledge and skill gaps. If the errors come from a confusing system, an unclear process or overload, retraining spends money without changing results, so the analysis must first establish the cause.
std
VII.B
A supervisor wants to see at a glance which operators are qualified on which workstations and where cover is thin. Which tool fits best?
An organization chart
A training needs survey
A course reaction form
A skills matrix

A skills matrix lists people against tasks or stations and shows each person’s qualification level, so gaps and single points of failure are easy to see. A survey gathers opinions about needs; it does not record verified qualification.
std
VII.B
A new regulation requires documented competence for staff who perform a certain test. How should the training needs analysis treat it?
As one topic among many, ranked against the others by how much interest staff show
As a need for managers only, since they are the ones who sign off the results
As met once the regulation has been circulated for the staff to read and sign
As a mandatory need that must be met and recorded, whatever staff preferences are

Regulatory requirements set needs that are not optional and must be evidenced, so they sit at the top of the analysis regardless of preference. Circulating the text does not show that anyone is competent to perform the test.
std
VII.B
A training gap analysis compares:
The training budget requested with the training budget approved
Course reaction scores from before and after a course is revised
The competence a role requires with the competence people now have
The number of courses offered this year with those offered last year
A gap analysis sets required competence against current competence; the difference is the training need. Budget and course counts describe the training function, not the workforce’s needs.
std
VII.B
A needs survey shows staff most want a time-management course, but performance reviews and audit findings point to weak root cause analysis. How should the training manager weigh these?
Weight the performance and audit gaps most, using the survey as one input
Follow the survey, since staff are the best judges of the training they need
Run both courses for everyone so that there is no need to choose between them
Discard the survey entirely because self-reported data cannot be trusted

Performance and audit evidence show gaps that affect results, so they carry more weight than stated preferences. The survey still adds information about motivation and needs people see in themselves, so discarding it is also wrong.
std
VII.C
Which design choice best applies adult learning principles to a course for experienced maintenance technicians?
Present the full theory first so they have the background before any practice
Build exercises around real problems and draw on their experience
Keep the sessions formal and hold all questions until the end of each module
Reuse the examples written for new hires so that all content stays consistent
Adults learn best when content is relevant to problems they face, involves them actively and uses the experience they bring. Long theory up front and one-way delivery work against those principles.
std
VII.C
New operators must learn to set up a complex press safely. Which delivery method fits best?
A self-paced e-learning module on press setup followed by a written test
On-the-job training with demonstration, supervised practice and sign-off
A classroom lecture that walks through photographs of each step of the setup
A workbook that operators study on their own before their first shift

A hands-on skill with safety risk is learned by watching it done, practicing under supervision and being signed off as competent. E-learning and reading can support the theory but cannot show that someone can perform the setup.
std
VII.C
Control room operators must practice their response to rare emergencies that cannot safely be staged on live equipment. Which delivery method fits best?
Simulation
On-the-job training
Self-directed reading
Classroom lecture

Simulation lets people practice realistic, high-risk scenarios without endangering people or equipment, and it can be repeated until the response is reliable. On-the-job training cannot be used when the event is rare and unsafe to create.
std
VII.C
Many people in a plant’s workforce speak English as a second language. Which change most improves training that relies on written work instructions?
Add visuals, demonstrations and plain language, and check understanding by practice
Lengthen the instructions so that every step is described in much more detail
Ask bilingual coworkers to explain the content informally after each class
Move the course to self-directed reading so people can work at their own pace

Visuals, demonstration and plain language reduce the load on reading, and practice confirms that people can do the task. Longer text makes the barrier worse, and informal explanations are inconsistent and unverified.
std
VII.C
After a course on structured problem solving, few participants use the method on the job. What would most improve transfer to the workplace?
Repeat the course with a longer and harder final examination
Have supervisors coach them as they apply it to real problems
Send each participant the course slides to keep as a reference
Extend the course with more time on the theory behind the method

Coaching on live problems bridges the gap between knowing a method and using it, and it signals that management expects it to be used. More theory or a harder test strengthens knowledge, which was not the gap.
std
VII.D
An end-of-course survey shows that 95% of participants were satisfied. In Kirkpatrick’s model, this is evidence at which level?
Level 2, learning
Level 3, behavior
Level 1, reaction
Level 4, results
Satisfaction ratings measure reaction, the first level. They say little about whether people learned (level 2), changed how they work (level 3) or improved business results (level 4).
std
VII.D
Test scores after a procedure course were high, but auditors find three months later that the procedure is not being followed. What does this suggest?
The test was too easy and should be made harder for the next group
Learning occurred but did not transfer; look for barriers in the workplace
The course failed to teach the procedure and must be fully redesigned
Three months is too soon to judge whether the training was effective

High test scores show learning (level 2); the audit shows no behavior change (level 3). The gap usually lies in the work environment, such as supervision, time pressure or incentives, rather than in the course.
std
VII.D
Which evidence best shows training effectiveness at the results level?
A fall in the department’s scrap rate after training, other causes ruled out
Post-test scores that are higher than the pre-test scores for the same group
Supervisors observing the new method in use on the line in the weeks after
Participants rating the course as highly useful on the end-of-course form

The results level looks at business outcomes such as scrap, cost or complaints, with care taken to separate the training’s effect from other changes. Observed use of the method is behavior, the level below results.
std
VII.D
A training program costs $40,000 and produces measured first-year benefits of $100,000. What is the training ROI?

ROI = (benefits − costs) / costs x 100 = (100,000 − 40,000) / 40,000 x 100 = 150%. 250% is the benefit-cost ratio (benefits / costs) shown as a percentage, which does not subtract the program cost from the benefits; 60% and 40% divide by benefits instead of costs.
std
VII.D
Post-test results show most learners miss the questions on one module, while the other modules score well. What should the training manager do?
Remove those test questions so that the scores better reflect the course as a whole
Put the learners who failed through the same module again until they pass it
Review that module’s content, delivery and test items to find the cause
Add more time to the whole course so that learners can absorb all of the material
A gap confined to one module points to that module: unclear content, weak delivery or flawed test items. Repeating it unchanged gives the same result, and removing the questions hides the problem.
std
I.A
In a company with many management layers, problems that operators report often reach senior leaders late and softened. Which feature of a tall hierarchy best explains this?
Spans of control are too wide for managers to supervise closely
Employees report to two bosses who give them conflicting direction
Decision authority sits mainly with front-line teams and supervisors
Information passes through many levels and is filtered at each one

Each added layer is another point where messages are delayed, summarized or softened, so tall structures slow and distort upward communication. Tall hierarchies have narrow, not wide, spans of control; dual reporting describes a matrix.
std
I.B.1
Engagement scores at a plant are low, and survey comments say employees' improvement ideas vanish without any response. What should the site leader do?
Set up a visible way to answer ideas and act on the worthwhile ones
Repeat the survey next quarter to confirm the low scores are real
Make engagement scores part of each supervisor's annual review
Run a poster campaign explaining why engagement matters to the plant

Leaders raise engagement by showing that people's input is heard and acted on, which removes the stated cause. Tying scores to supervisor reviews pressures managers but does nothing about the ignored ideas.
std
I.B.2
A quality manager sets next year's department objectives, chooses the projects that will meet them and estimates the resources each will need. Which management function is this?
Directing
Organizing
Planning
Controlling
Setting objectives and deciding how and with what resources to reach them is planning. Controlling comes later, when results are compared with those objectives and gaps are corrected.
std
I.B.2
A quality manager determines that the lab needs two more certified technicians, recruits them and arranges their training. Which management function is she mainly performing?
Directing
Staffing
Controlling
Coordinating
Staffing covers filling positions with competent people: recruiting, selecting, placing and training them. Directing concerns guiding and motivating people once they are in their jobs.
std
I.B.2
A supervisor holds daily huddles to explain priorities, coaches operators who are struggling and encourages the team to hit its targets. Which management function is this mainly?
Planning
Directing
Organizing
Controlling
Directing (leading) is guiding, coaching and motivating people to carry out the plan. Organizing is arranging jobs, reporting lines and resources, which is not what the huddles do.
std
I.B.3

A CEO announces a major quality transformation by email. Six months later little has changed, and middle managers say they never saw a reason to change. Which step of Kotter's model was most likely skipped?
Anchoring new approaches in the culture
Generating visible short-term wins
Consolidating gains to produce more change
Establishing a sense of urgency

Kotter's first step is building a sense of urgency so people see why change is needed; managers who see no reason to change point to that gap. Anchoring in the culture is the last step and cannot happen before people accept the need.
std
I.B.3
A force field analysis for a new scheduling system shows strong restraining forces, chiefly operators' fear of losing their jobs. Following the logic of the tool, what is usually most effective?
Reduce the restraining forces, such as by addressing job security fears
Add pressure from senior leaders to strengthen the driving forces
List more driving forces so their total outweighs the restraining side
Drop the change, since the restraining forces are now the stronger side

Lewin observed that weakening restraining forces usually moves a change with less tension than pushing harder, which tends to raise resistance. Adding pressure is the tempting choice but often hardens opposition.
std
I.B.3
A new regulation in a key export market will require full material traceability on all parts shipped there within a year. What should the quality manager do first?
Wait until customers in that market ask for traceability before acting
Add the requirement to the quality manual and tell the sites to comply
Stop shipping to that market until the new regulation takes effect
Assess the gap between current traceability and the new requirement

Responding to an external change starts with understanding its impact on current processes so a realistic plan can be made. Simply writing the requirement into the manual issues a demand without knowing what must change.
std
I.B.3
Which change effort is the clearest example of transformational rather than incremental change?
Cutting setup time on one press by improving the changeover method
Updating a work instruction to add one new inspection step
Shifting from selling products to selling services, with new structure and culture
Replacing a worn gauge with a newer model of the same type
Transformational change alters the organization's strategy, structure or culture as a whole. The other options are small improvements within the existing way of working, which is incremental change.
std
I.B.3
Six months after a new corrective action process was introduced, the quality director wants to know whether the change worked. Which evidence is most meaningful?
Recurrence rates and closure times compared with the baseline
The number of employees who completed training on the new process
Whether the new procedure was approved and posted on schedule
How many corrective actions have been opened since the launch
A change is effective if it improves the outcomes it was meant to improve, judged against the baseline. Training completions show the change was deployed, not that it worked.
std
I.B.4
An operator worried about rumored layoffs shows little interest in a new recognition program. Which explanation is most consistent with Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
Unmet safety needs, such as job security, come before esteem needs
Recognition is a hygiene factor and cannot motivate on its own
Self-actualization needs must be met before esteem needs matter
Esteem needs are met only by pay, not by recognition from other people

Maslow held that lower needs such as safety and security dominate until reasonably met, so recognition (an esteem need) has little pull for someone fearing job loss. Calling recognition a hygiene factor mixes up Herzberg, who classed it as a motivator.
std
I.B.4
A plant manager believes most people want to do good work and will take responsibility when given the chance. Which practice best fits this Theory Y view?
Use detailed rules and close supervision to prevent shirking
Tie all pay to output so that people are pushed to work harder
Give teams clear goals and let them decide how to meet them
Require a supervisor to sign off on every operator decision
McGregor's Theory Y assumes people are self-directed and seek responsibility, which supports goal setting with autonomy. Close supervision and output pressure follow from Theory X assumptions.
std
I.B.4
