Six months into a quality initiative, employees say they no longer hear how it is going or whether their effort matters. What will best sustain their enthusiasm?
Relaunch the initiative under a fresh name and a new slogan
Hold a one-time celebration lunch for all employees at the site
Share regular progress results and link them to people's work
Add the initiative's goals to every employee's annual appraisal
Enthusiasm lasts when people see progress and how their own contribution drives it, which addresses the stated complaint. A one-time event gives a brief lift but leaves people uninformed afterward.
std
I.B.4
Before negotiating a price increase demanded by a sole-source supplier, a team qualifies a second source as a fallback. In negotiation terms, what have they strengthened?
Their opening anchor for the price discussion
The supplier's own walk-away point in the talks
Their stated position on the payment terms
Their walk-away alternative (BATNA)
A qualified second source is a better alternative if talks fail (a stronger BATNA), which increases leverage. An opening anchor is the first offer made, which the team has not changed.
std
I.B.4
A manager is told that a new training program cut defects by 40% because defects fell after it began. Applying critical thinking, what should she ask first?
Whether something else changed at the same time that could explain it
How many employees enjoyed the training and would recommend it
Whether the program could be rolled out to the other plants by next quarter
How much the program cost for each employee who was trained
Critical thinking tests the causal claim: a drop after training does not prove the training caused it, so other changes must be ruled out. Rollout and cost questions assume the claim is already true.
std
I.B.5
A plant manager wants line teams to stop the line when they find quality problems. Which step is most important to make this empowerment work?
Require a supervisor's approval before any team can stop the line
Tell teams they are empowered and let them work out the details
Rank teams by fewest line stops and post the results each week
Define clear limits of authority and back teams when they use it
Empowerment needs clear boundaries and visible management support so people trust they can act. Telling teams they are empowered without defining limits leaves them unsure and unwilling to act.
std
I.B.5
A quality manager is restructuring inspector jobs. Which statement correctly distinguishes job design from job tasks?
Job design lists each step of the work; job tasks state the job's overall purpose
Job design sets the pay grade of a job; job tasks set its hours and shift pattern
Job design combines tasks, duties and authority into a job; tasks are units of work
Job design applies only to managers; job tasks apply only to front-line staff
Job design is the deliberate structuring of what a job contains and how it is done, built from individual tasks. The first distractor reverses the two ideas.
std
I.C.1
Which type of team has as its main purpose studying an existing process, finding the causes of its problems and making lasting improvements to it?
Self-managed team
Work group
Executive steering committee
Process improvement team
A process improvement team is formed to analyze and improve a specific process. A self-managed team runs its own day-to-day work rather than being chartered to improve a process.
std
I.C.1
Management forms a team to plan the move of the test lab to a new building. The team will disband as soon as the move is complete. This is a:
Self-managed team
Temporary (ad hoc) team
Work group
Quality steering committee
A temporary or ad hoc team is formed for one special project and disbands when it ends. A work group is a standing unit of people under one supervisor.
std
I.C.1
Four members of an audit team work together at the plant, while three others join every meeting by video from other sites. This team is best described as a:
Cross-functional team
Self-managed team
Work group
Hybrid team

A hybrid team mixes members who work together in person with members who take part remotely. A fully virtual team works almost entirely through technology, with members rarely together, which does not fit four members sharing a site.
std
I.C.2

After a period of conflict, team members have agreed on ground rules, share information freely and are building trust, but still check with the leader on key decisions. Which stage and leadership approach fit?
Storming; restate the ground rules and settle disputes for them
Norming; encourage the team and share more of the decisions
Forming; give clear direction on purpose, roles and goals
Performing; delegate fully and step back from the work

Agreed norms and growing trust mark norming, where the leader supports and gradually shares decision making. Full delegation suits performing, which the team has not reached while it still relies on the leader.
std
I.C.4
What is the main responsibility of a team facilitator?
Making the final decision for the team whenever members cannot agree
Providing resources and removing barriers across the organization
Helping the team use sound process and tools without steering content
Owning the process and sustaining its results after the project ends
A facilitator guides how the team works, such as meeting process, participation and tools, and stays neutral on content. Providing resources and removing barriers is the champion's job.
std
I.C.4
Which responsibility belongs mainly to the team leader rather than to the champion?
Securing budget and resources from senior management
Running meetings and directing day-to-day work
Removing barriers that lie outside the team's control
Approving the charter and project scope at launch
The team leader manages the team's work and meetings. The champion (sponsor) works at the organizational level: approving the charter, securing resources and removing outside barriers.
std
I.C.4
On a large improvement project, who is mainly responsible for planning the schedule, budget and resources and tracking progress against them?
Team facilitator
Champion
Project manager
Process owner
The project manager plans and controls schedule, cost and resources. The champion provides resources and support but does not run day-to-day project tracking.
std
I.C.4
What is expected of a contributor (team member) on an improvement team?
Bring expertise, complete assigned actions and take part in decisions
Guide the meeting process while staying strictly neutral on the content
Own the process and sustain the gains after the project closes
Set direction and remove barriers that lie outside the team
Contributors supply knowledge, do the assigned work and take part in team decisions. Guiding process neutrally is the facilitator's role, and sustaining gains belongs to the process owner.
std
I.C.4
Meetings of a process team often drift into complaints about parking and the cafeteria. Which practice best keeps the team on task?
Cancel meetings until members agree to stay focused
Use a timed agenda and a parking lot
Let the discussion run so members feel they are heard
Have the leader decide each item without discussion
A timed agenda with a parking lot keeps discussion on the team's purpose while still capturing other concerns. Letting the drift continue wastes the team's time and does not resolve the complaints.
std
I.C.4
One team member often interrupts others and dismisses their ideas, and quieter members have stopped speaking. What should the team leader do?
Ignore it, since confronting him may only make the problem worse
Ask the sponsor to remove him from the team without telling him the reason
Address the behavior, cite the ground rules and draw out quieter members
Give him the team leader role so that his energy is put to good use
Disruptive behavior should be dealt with promptly and constructively, using the agreed ground rules, while restoring balanced participation. Ignoring it lets it continue and keeps others silent.
std
I.D.1
A quality engineer leaves a company and joins a competitor. His new manager asks him for his former employer's supplier cost data. What should he do?
Share it, since he no longer works for the former employer
Share only the figures he personally helped to compile
Decline for now, but share it once any non-compete period has ended
Decline, as the data belong to his former employer

I.D.1

A quality manager finds that a shipped batch may have a defect that could injure users. The sales director wants to wait until next quarter to avoid hurting results. What does the spirit of the ASQ Code of Ethics require?
Put user safety first and press for prompt containment and notice
Wait as the sales director asks, since sales owns the customer
Notify customers only if a user is actually reported injured
Correct future batches quietly and leave the batch already shipped alone
The code puts public health and safety ahead of business results, so a possible injury hazard calls for prompt action. Waiting for an actual injury accepts a risk the code asks members to prevent.
std
I.D.1
During an audit closing meeting, an auditor openly mocks a supervisor's accent and ridicules the department's work. Which ethical principle is most at issue?
Protecting confidential information from the audit
Respect and fair treatment of others
Avoiding conflicts of interest with the auditee
Keeping one's professional competence current
Ridiculing people breaches the duty to treat others with respect and fairness. No confidential information or conflict of interest is involved in the scenario.

Accept it if the work is done only on her own time
Accept it if she uses none of her employer's equipment
Disclose the offer and get approval before accepting
Disclose it after the first assignment, once she knows the work suits her

Outside work for a competitor is a potential conflict of interest that policies require be disclosed and approved in advance. Doing it on her own time does not remove the conflict of loyalties, and disclosure after the work starts is too late.

Whether privacy law and policy allow the transfer, and on what terms
Whether the file is small enough to send as an email attachment
Whether the analytics firm has done similar work for the company before
Whether the complaint records cover a full calendar year of data

I.D.2
A plant's air permit limits solvent emissions. A process change would raise output but push emissions above the permit limit. What should the quality manager advise?
Run the change and pay any fine, since a fine costs less than the lost output
Run the change but report the emissions only as an annual average
Hold the change only until the annual emissions report has been filed
Hold the change until the permit is amended or emissions are controlled

Operating above a permit limit breaks environmental law, so the change must wait for an amended permit or added controls. Treating fines as a cost of doing business is still knowing noncompliance, and the timing of a report does not change the limit.

Board independence and oversight of executive pay
Fair labor practices for supplier workers
Reducing energy use and carbon emissions at plants
Anti-bribery controls and audit committee review
The social element covers how a company treats people: workers, suppliers' workforces, customers and communities. Board independence and anti-bribery controls belong to governance.

A quality agreement
A certificate of conformance
A supplier scorecard

Refuse, since the design is the supplier's protected property
Allow it, since the customer paid for parts made with the tool
Refuse for now, but allow it once the current parts contract ends
Allow it if the new supplier also signs a non-disclosure agreement

The design is the supplier’s intellectual property, shared only for the review under an NDA, so passing it on would breach that agreement now or after the contract ends. A new NDA with another supplier does not give the customer the right to share it.

II.A

Vision statement
Mission statement
Values statement
Strategic objective

II.A

Mission, tactic, strategic objective
Strategic objective, vision, tactic
Vision, strategic objective, tactic
Vision, tactic, strategic objective

The first is an aspirational future state (vision), the second is a measurable multi-year goal (strategic objective), and the third is a specific, near-term action that supports the goal (tactic). Calling the market-share goal a tactic reverses the hierarchy: tactics serve objectives.

II.B.1

Our bottling line is 25 years old and slow
Local demand for craft beer keeps growing
Our brewmaster has won several awards
A national brewer is building a plant nearby

Technological

Political
Economic
Social
Technological

Interest rates, inflation, exchange rates and business cycles are economic factors. Central-bank and government actions may sit behind the rates, but the effect on customer buying is economic, not political.

II.B.1
A spare-parts distributor's PESTLE analysis notes that low-cost additive manufacturing lets customers print some replacement parts on site. Which PESTLE factor is this?
Environmental
Economic
Technological
Social
New production methods such as additive manufacturing are technological factors. The change may have economic effects on the distributor, but its source is a technology shift.

II.B.1
A food company's PESTLE analysis notes that a new law will require every package to list the country of origin of each ingredient. Which PESTLE factor is this?
Political
Economic
Environmental
Legal
Laws and regulations that the company must follow are legal factors. Political factors cover government stability and policy direction; once a requirement is enacted as law, it is analyzed as legal.

II.B.1
A PESTLE analysis notes that more frequent coastal flooding threatens a key warehouse and the roads that serve it. Which PESTLE factor is this?
Environmental
Technological
Social
Political
Climate, weather and natural-resource conditions are environmental factors. The flooding may lead to new rules later, but today it is a physical, environmental risk.

II.B.1
A strategic risk review rates the loss of the company's largest customer, which provides 40% of revenue, as unlikely. How should the team treat this risk?
Drop it from the plan, since its likelihood is low
Plan mitigation, such as widening the customer base
Accept it, since customer decisions are external
Raise prices to that customer to offset exposure

Risk analysis weighs impact as well as likelihood; a low-probability event that would remove 40% of revenue warrants a mitigation or contingency plan. Dropping it because it is unlikely ignores the severity of the consequence.

In a mature market, several firms of similar size sell nearly identical products, growth is slow and exit costs are high. Which of Porter's five forces is strongest here?
Threat of substitute goods
Power of the suppliers
Rivalry among existing firms
Threat of new entrants

Supplier power; qualify alternate material sources
Rivalry; match the lowest competitor's price
Substitutes; redesign the parts for new uses
Buyer power; broaden the customer base over time

A single customer buying most of the output holds strong bargaining power, and reducing dependence on that customer weakens it. Qualifying alternate materials addresses supplier power, which is not the problem described.

II.B.2
Economists forecast a recession over the next 18 months. A capital-equipment maker's sales usually fall sharply in downturns. What should its strategic plan include?
Scenarios that adjust capacity and cash to demand
An expansion plan based on last year's growth rate
A freeze on all quality improvement activity
Price increases to offset lost sales volume

Economic conditions should shape the plan through scenarios and triggers for capacity, inventory and cash. Planning on last year's growth ignores a known economic force, and raising prices in a downturn usually deepens the volume loss.
std
II.B.2

Raising export prices to protect margins
Producing or partnering inside the bloc
Treating it as outside the plan's scope
Waiting for customers to raise the issue

A global market change that gives competitors inside the bloc a tariff advantage calls for a strategic response such as local production or partnerships. Raising export prices would worsen the cost gap the tariffs already create.
std
II.B.2
A company wants to grow revenue 50% in five years. It holds a strong share of a market that is shrinking about 5% per year. What does this positioning suggest?
Its present market alone can supply the growth
Its strong share means no strategy change is needed
Most growth must come from new markets or products
Price cuts will reverse the market's decline

If the market shrinks 5% a year, it will be about 77% of today's size in five years, so a 50% revenue gain would require nearly doubling market share. The firm is poorly positioned for growth in its current market and needs new markets or products.

II.B.2
Customers in a company's market now expect next-day delivery and online order tracking, which the company does not offer. How should the strategic plan respond?
Wait until customers file formal complaints
Stress product quality, which customers value most
Lower prices to offset the slower delivery
Treat it as a new requirement and close the gap

Rising expectations turn yesterday's extras into basic requirements, so the plan should treat the gap as a strategic risk and close it. Waiting for complaints means reacting after customers have already started to leave.

During stakeholder analysis for a hospital expansion, which concern should the team expect to be primary for nearby residents?
Traffic, noise and access around the site
Return on the hospital's invested capital
Nurse staffing ratios and shift schedules
Reimbursement rates paid by insurers

Neighbors are external stakeholders whose main concerns are the local effects of construction and operation. Staffing ratios matter most to employees and patients, and return on capital matters most to owners and lenders.

Short: new cost position; long: startup disruption
Short: startup disruption; long: new cost position
Short: workforce skills; long: training schedule
Short: market share gain; long: installation work

In the short term, new technology brings installation, debugging and retraining disruption; over the long term it changes the cost structure and capability the strategy can build on. The other pairings place near-term transition effects in the long term.

II.B.4
A bottling line is redesigned so robots fill, cap and label bottles with no operator involvement, but the line has no ability to detect defects or stop itself. This is an example of:
Autonomation
Error-proofing
Automation
Andon signaling
Automation replaces human effort with machines. Autonomation (jidoka) adds the ability to detect an abnormal condition and stop, which this line lacks, so it is plain automation.

II.B.4
A quality manager proposes a Quality 4.0 initiative. Which project best fits that label?
Add a second shift of final product inspectors
Update paper work instructions with new photos
Move internal audits to an annual schedule only
Link machine sensor data to real-time SPC alerts

Quality 4.0 applies Industry 4.0 technologies such as connected sensors, analytics and automation to quality management. Adding inspectors or updating paper instructions may help, but they are conventional methods, not digital transformation.
std
II.B.4
A plant connects its production equipment to the corporate network for remote monitoring. Which strategic risk does this most directly add?
Cyberattacks that halt or alter production
Higher turnover among skilled machine operators
Longer changeover times on connected machines
Loss of certification to the quality standard

Connecting operational technology to a network exposes it to cyberattacks that can stop equipment or change settings and product. Certification loss is not a direct consequence of networking equipment; it would follow only from failures in the quality system.
std
II.B.5
A firm's strategy is to win contracts that require Cpk of at least 1.33 on critical features. Its process capability studies show Cpk of 0.9. What should the internal capability analysis conclude?
The process meets the need with margin
Process improvement is needed first
Adding inspectors alone will qualify it
The requirement is for suppliers only

A Cpk of 0.9 is well below the 1.33 required, so operational capability is a gap the strategy must close through process improvement before bidding. Added inspection may sort out defects, but it does not raise process capability, which is what the customer requires.
std
II.C.1
Reviewing a deployment plan, a quality manager finds that strategic objective 3 has no tactics assigned, while two department tactics support no objective. What should she recommend?
Approve the plan, since most objectives are covered
Remove objective 3 from this year's strategic plan
Add tactics for objective 3; relink or drop the others
Ask each department to add tactics to all objectives

Every strategic objective needs tactics that move it, and every tactic should trace to an objective; the plan fails on both counts. Approving it leaves one objective with no means of achievement and spends resources on work that serves no objective.

II.C.2
A strategy calls for Six Sigma projects in every plant, but a skills review finds only two trained Black Belts in the company. What should leadership do before launch?
Launch everywhere and let teams learn by doing
Hire consultants to run every project for good
Drop the statistical methods from the initiative
Plan training and coaching to build the skills

Deployment requires that people have the competence to carry out their part, so leadership should build skills through training and coaching before or alongside launch. Launching without skills risks failed projects and loss of credibility for the initiative.
std
II.C.2

Leadership approves a strategic initiative to cut lead time 50% by the end of next year, but next year's budget has no funds for it; each department's budget was copied from last year. What does this show?
Budgets are not aligned to the plan
The lead-time target fails the SMART test
Departments are overspending their budgets
The goal should be funded from future savings

Strategic priorities need resources, and a budget rolled forward from last year cannot fund new initiatives. The target is specific, measurable and time-bound, so the problem is resource allocation, not the SMART criteria.

II.C.3
At a quarterly strategy review, on-time delivery is 88% against a plan target of 95%, up from a baseline of 85%. What is the best interpretation?
The objective is met, since delivery improved
It improved but lags plan; analyze the gap
Lower the target to 88% for the rest of the year
The measure is invalid because it missed target

Delivery has gained 3 of the 10 planned points (30% of the planned improvement), so progress is real but behind plan and the gap should be analyzed and acted on. Lowering the target to current performance abandons the strategic goal.

Approval of the measure wording by the CEO
A link to every employee's annual bonus plan
A definition, baseline, target, owner and frequency
A spot in each department's monthly newsletter to staff

A usable measure needs an operational definition of what is counted and how, a baseline, a target, an owner and a reporting frequency. CEO approval of the wording does not make the measure measurable.

In hoshin kanri, how are breakthrough objectives handled compared with routine work?
Every departmental goal is promoted to a breakthrough objective each year
Each department sets its own breakthrough goals with no top-level input
Daily management is paused until the breakthrough objectives are met
A vital few get focused deployment; routine work goes to daily management

Hoshin kanri concentrates effort on a vital few breakthrough objectives and deploys them through catchball, while routine performance is sustained through daily management. Making every goal a breakthrough goal defeats the focus the method depends on.
std
II.C.4
A quality manager has 20 proposed improvement projects and capacity for six. Which selection approach best supports strategic deployment?
Score each project on impact to strategic objectives
Fund the projects whose sponsors are most senior
Choose the six quickest projects for early wins
Spread capacity across all 20 to keep people engaged

Selecting projects by their contribution to strategic objectives directs limited capacity where it moves the plan. Picking the quickest projects can give early wins, but it ignores whether they advance the strategy.

Assign each supervisor a share of the returns and review them monthly
Set measurable objectives and plan the actions to meet them
Hire two more final inspectors to stop returns before they ship
Recognize the teams with the fewest returns at the next town hall

Planning means setting objectives and deciding how, when and with what they will be met. Assigning targets and reviewing them monthly belongs to organizing and controlling, and it skips the plan those functions depend on.

III.A.1
A plant has a sound improvement plan and clearly assigned roles, but employees are skeptical and progress is slow. Which management function most needs attention?
Leading
Planning
Organizing
Controlling

Leading is about communicating the vision, motivating and influencing people so they commit to the plan. The plan and the roles already exist, so more planning or organizing would not address the skepticism that is holding progress back.

After a merger, two inspection groups report to different managers, duplicate some checks and leave other checks undone. Which management function addresses this most directly?
Controlling
Leading
Planning
Organizing

Organizing sets the structure: who does which work and who reports to whom, which is what overlaps and gaps in inspection reflect. Controlling would detect the resulting deviations but would not fix the structure that causes them.
std
III.A.2
A company relies on a clear hierarchy, written rules, defined positions and hiring based on qualifications, so work is done the same way whoever holds a job. Which theory does this reflect?
Mayo’s human relations theory
Senge’s systems thinking
Weber’s bureaucratic theory
Hersey and Blanchard’s situational leadership

Weber’s bureaucratic model, part of classical organizational theory, stresses hierarchy, formal rules, defined roles and selection on merit. Human relations theory focuses instead on social needs and informal groups at work.

III.A.2
A manager believes most employees like responsibility and will direct themselves toward goals they are committed to, so she gives her teams wide latitude. Which theory does this reflect?
McGregor’s Theory X
McGregor’s Theory Y
Taylor’s scientific management
Weber’s bureaucratic theory

Theory Y assumes people find work natural, seek responsibility and exercise self-direction toward goals they accept. Theory X is the opposite assumption, that people dislike work and must be closely directed and controlled.

III.A.2
A company holds after-action reviews, encourages small experiments and spreads what it learns so it keeps adapting to change. Which management concept best describes its aim?
Learning organization
Scientific management
Bureaucratic organization
Management by exception

A learning organization, as described by Senge, continually builds its capacity to learn and adapt through shared learning and systems thinking. Scientific management seeks one best method and fixes it, which is the opposite of continual adaptation.
std
III.A.2

Span of control
Management by objectives
Scientific management
Systems thinking

Systems thinking looks at how parts of an organization interact, so it would flag that cutting inspection shifts cost downstream to warranty. Management by objectives helps set and track targets, but by itself it does not reveal side effects in other parts of the system.

III.A.2
A manager enters a new market where cause and effect are unclear and past best practices may not apply. Which approach fits this situation best?
Apply the proven home-market procedure without any change
Delay all action until complete data on the market exist
Run small, safe trials and adapt as patterns emerge
Hire an outside expert and follow his fixed method exactly

In complex situations the right answer cannot be known in advance, so managers probe with small experiments, watch what happens and amplify what works. Applying a fixed best practice assumes the cause-and-effect relationships are already known, which is not the case here.

III.A.2

Participative, and it fits because the team follows a shared plan
Autocratic, and it suits an emergency with no time for input
Autocratic, and it is wrong because it bypasses employee involvement
Transformational, and it fits because it inspires rapid action

III.A.2

Participative
Autocratic
Transactional
Laissez-faire

III.A.2

Transactional
Autocratic
Bureaucratic
Transformational

Transformational leaders motivate through vision, inspiration and intellectual challenge. Transactional leaders rely on exchanging rewards for meeting set targets, not on changing how people see their work.
std
III.A.2
Two supervisors disagree about whether a new fixture reduced defects, and each cites his own impressions. What should the manager do to apply management by fact?
Side with the more experienced supervisor, since he knows the line
Keep the fixture, since its purchase cost has already been spent
Compare defect data from before and after the change, then decide
Have the operators vote on whether the fixture should be kept
Management by fact means decisions rest on data and analysis rather than opinion. Deferring to seniority still decides on impressions, just the impressions of a different person.
std
III.A.2

Do the analysis himself and have her present the conclusions
Ask guiding questions and give feedback as she works
Set a deadline and review only the final report she submits
Give her a fixed script and require her to follow every step

Coaching develops the person by guiding her reasoning through questions and timely feedback while she does the work. A fixed script directs rather than develops, and doing the work for her teaches nothing.

III.A.2
A manager moves from a 40-person startup in a fast-changing software market to a large, heavily regulated pharmaceutical plant. How should her management style most likely change?
More weight on defined procedures, documentation and compliance
More informal decisions made quickly without written records
Less attention to regulation, since the plant is long established
No change, since a sound style works the same way everywhere

Size, industry and regulation shape the fitting style: a large regulated plant needs formal procedures, records and controls. Keeping the same style everywhere ignores the contingency view that context drives the right approach.

III.A.3
Engineering is introducing a new process that requires certified welders by next quarter. Which function must engineering coordinate with most closely to have qualified people in place?
Marketing
Finance
Logistics
Human resources
Human resources recruits, trains and tracks qualifications, so it must plan the welder certification with engineering. Finance may fund the training but does not find or qualify the people.

III.A.3
Engineering is designing a next-generation product. Which function’s input is most needed to make sure the design reflects what target customers value?
Purchasing
Logistics
Marketing
Finance
Marketing gathers market research and the voice of the customer that should drive design requirements. Purchasing matters for sourcing parts, but it does not define what customers value.
std
III.A.3
Finance stretches payment terms to suppliers from 30 to 90 days to improve cash flow. Which effect should the quality manager watch for?
Fewer customer complaints as cash is freed for marketing work
Strained suppliers delivering late or poorer-quality parts
Lower inspection costs as suppliers absorb more of the work
Faster engineering change approvals across the supply base

Slower payment squeezes suppliers’ cash, which can lead them to cut corners or fall behind, and that reaches the plant as quality and delivery problems. There is no mechanism by which longer terms would make suppliers take on more inspection.
std
III.A.3
R&D hands a new design to production without involving manufacturing engineers, and the launch suffers high scrap. Which practice would most likely have prevented this?
Concurrent engineering with early production input
Heavier final inspection during the first weeks of the launch
A larger R&D budget to fund additional prototype testing
Tighter tolerances on the drawings to reduce part variation
Involving production early lets design account for manufacturing capability before the design is fixed. Extra inspection only sorts the scrap that the design is already creating.
std
III.A.3
The plant is replacing its enterprise resource planning (ERP) system. Why should quality be involved in setting the requirements?
IT cannot legally select software without quality’s approval
Quality normally owns the IT budget for plant-wide systems
Quality staff are the main users of the accounting module
Traceability and nonconformance records depend on it

IT systems carry the records the quality system relies on, such as traceability, holds and nonconformances, so a poor setup degrades quality processes. There is no legal requirement for quality to approve software selection.
std
III.A.3
Logistics starts holding finished goods until it can ship full truckloads, to cut freight costs. What is the most likely effect on customers?
Fewer defects found in the parts they receive
Lower warranty claims from products in the field
Longer, less predictable delivery times
Shorter lead times for the plant’s raw materials

III.A.3

More spare connectors stocked in every service technician’s van
A feedback loop that sends field failure data to engineering
A longer warranty period on the connector to reassure users
A separate service budget to cover connector replacements
Service sees failures first, and routing that data to engineering lets the root cause be designed out. Stocking more spares makes repairs faster but leaves the failure in every unit built.
std
III.A.4

Regular check-ins with notes kept through the year
Ranking all employees against each other on a forced curve
Having employees write their own reviews with no manager input
Shortening the review form so it takes less time to complete

Recency bias comes from relying on memory, and documented check-ins give a record of the whole period. Forced ranking changes how ratings are distributed but still rests on the same recent impressions.

III.A.4

More advanced statistics courses to deepen her existing strength
A raise that depends on her staying in her current technical role
A transfer to a role with no supervisory duties for now
Leadership training and a stretch role leading a project team

Development should close the gap between current skills and the goal, here leadership, through training and supervised experience. More statistics builds a strength she already has rather than the skills the new role needs.
std
III.A.5

$3.9 million
$0.7 million
$2.1 million

Analyze the variance, forecast spend and propose offsets
Stop all calibration work until the new fiscal year begins
Charge the extra calibration cost to production’s budget
Wait until year end and explain the overrun at that point

The number of supplier audits the program will add this year
The statistical methods the team will use to analyze suppliers
The ISO 9001 clauses that the program will help the plant meet
The cost of poor quality it removes and the expected payback

III.A.5
