III.A.5
A project’s internal rate of return is 14%, and the company’s hurdle rate is 10%. What does this tell the quality manager?
It will pay back its full cost in about seven years
Its NPV at 10% is positive, so it clears the hurdle rate
It returns 4% more than its cost in each year of its life
It will earn 14% on total assets in the income statement

IRR is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero, so discounting at a lower rate such as 10% gives a positive NPV and the project meets the hurdle. IRR says nothing directly about payback time or accounting returns on assets.
std
III.A.5
A quality council must choose among a dozen improvement projects with limited funds. How should it apply portfolio analysis?
Rate value, risk and strategic fit, then fund the best mix
Fund each project in the order in which it was first submitted
Fund the largest projects first, since they are likely to matter most
Split the funds so that every department gets one project funded
Portfolio analysis looks at projects together, weighing return, risk and alignment to choose the set that best uses limited resources. Funding by size assumes cost equals value, which it does not.
std
III.A.6
Under ISO 31000, after risks have been identified and analyzed, which step decides which risks need treatment?
Risk monitoring
Risk communication
Establishing the context
Risk evaluation

In ISO 31000, risk assessment runs identification, analysis and evaluation; evaluation compares results with the risk criteria to decide what needs treatment. Monitoring and review runs throughout the process but does not make that decision.
std
III.A.6
A product launch depends on one tooling supplier delivering a mold in week 10, and that task is on the critical path. What is the best risk response?
Log the risk in the register and review it at project closure
Plan to compress later tasks if and when the mold arrives late
Track the supplier’s progress closely and line up a backup source
Ask the customer now to accept a launch that is several weeks late
A single-point schedule risk on the critical path calls for early warning and a contingency ready to use. Reviewing it at closure is too late to protect the launch date.
std
III.A.6
Receiving accepts material based only on the packing slip, and wrong-grade steel has reached production twice. Which control fits best?
Ask suppliers to print packing slips in larger, bolder type
Verify material identity and certifications before release
Add heavier inspection of finished parts at final test
Reduce the approved steel suppliers to a single source

The risk enters at receiving, so the control belongs there: confirm grade and certification before material moves on. Final inspection may catch some wrong material, but only after it has been processed.
std
III.A.6
Most of a plant’s revenue comes from one customer, who has started paying invoices late. Which type of risk is this mainly?
Financial risk
Product safety risk
Regulatory compliance risk
Process capability risk

Dependence on one customer and slow payment threaten cash flow and income, which is financial risk (credit and concentration). Nothing in the situation involves product safety, regulation or process performance.
std
III.A.6
A single CNC machine is the only one able to make a critical part, and it has no maintenance plan and no backup. Which risk-based action fits best?
Insure the machine and accept any downtime that may follow
Run the machine harder now to build a very large safety stock
Wait for a breakdown before deciding whether a backup is needed
Start preventive maintenance and qualify an alternate source
Preventive maintenance lowers the likelihood of failure and an alternate source limits the impact if it happens. Insurance pays for repair but does not keep the customer supplied during the downtime.
std
III.A.6
Field data show that users are sometimes burned when they open a product’s service panel while the unit is hot. Under the hierarchy of controls, which response is the most effective?
Add a warning label to the outside of the service panel
Add a caution about hot surfaces to the user manual
Redesign so the panel cannot open until the unit has cooled
Advise users to wear gloves when opening the panel
The hierarchy of controls puts eliminating or engineering out a hazard ahead of warnings and protective equipment. A label relies on users noticing and heeding it, so it is a weaker control.
std
III.A.6
A supervisor wants to switch to a new cleaning solvent that a vendor says works better. What should happen before the switch?
Use it on one shift and switch back if any problems show up
Assess its effects on product and safety via change control
Approve the switch, since the vendor guarantees the solvent
Let the supervisor decide, since cleaning is a minor task
Even small changes can affect residue, adhesion or worker safety, so they should be assessed and approved before use. Trying it on one shift exposes product and people to an unassessed change.
std
III.A.7
A knowledge management program wants to protect the organization’s core competencies first. Which knowledge fits that description?
Know-how that customers value and rivals find hard to copy
General office procedures common to most companies
Skills that can easily be bought from outside providers
Information already published in industry standards

A core competency delivers customer value and is difficult for competitors to imitate, so it is the knowledge most worth capturing and protecting. Skills that can be bought easily offer no lasting advantage.
std
III.A.7
Which of these is an example of explicit knowledge?
An operator’s feel for when a weld sounds wrong
A veteran buyer’s sense of which suppliers to trust
An engineer’s intuition about where a design will fail
A documented setup procedure with photos and settings
Explicit knowledge has been written down or recorded so others can access it, as in a documented procedure. The other options are tacit knowledge held in people’s experience and hard to write down.
std
III.A.7
Several suppliers make the same recurring error when interpreting a drawing note. Which knowledge-sharing practice would help most?
A separate corrective action request each time an error occurs
Keeping the lesson internal to protect design information
A supplier forum to share the lesson and the correct practice
Replacing every supplier that has made the error
Sharing the lesson with the whole supply base prevents the error at suppliers who have not yet made it. Issuing corrective actions one by one handles each case after the fact and repeats the effort.
std
III.A.7
Maintenance technicians at four plants solve similar equipment problems independently. Which KM technique would best connect them?
A rule that corporate engineering must approve all repairs
A community of practice that meets and shares solutions
A yearly award for the plant with the lowest downtime
A central library holding all the equipment manuals

A community of practice links people who do similar work so they share both tacit and explicit know-how. A manual library holds only explicit vendor information and not the fixes technicians have found.
std
III.B.1
A quality manager must tell suppliers about a new requirement for certificate of conformance content that takes effect in 60 days. Which mode of communication is essential?
A written notice stating the requirement, effective date and contact
A phone call to each supplier’s sales representative
A brief mention at the annual supplier day
A slide shown at the next quarterly business review

A requirement with a date needs a written record that suppliers can refer to and that shows they were told. A phone call may help, but it leaves no reference copy and depends on the representative passing it on accurately.
std
III.B.1
Operators on a fast-paced line often miss process changes announced in long memos. Which approach is most likely to help?
Longer memos that explain the reasons for each change in detail
An email sent to all operators each time a change is made
A quarterly meeting to review all of the changes made
Visual displays at each workstation showing the change
Visual communication at the point of use gets the key information to people who cannot stop to read. A longer memo adds to the reading burden that is causing operators to miss changes.
std
III.B.1
In hybrid meetings, remote participants rarely speak, and decisions are made by the people in the room. What should the meeting leader do?
Hold all decisions until remote members can travel to the site
Ask remote members to email their comments after the meeting
Invite remote members by name and share materials on screen
Limit the meeting to people who can attend it in person
Hybrid meetings need deliberate steps so remote people can see the same material and have a real turn to speak. Comments sent after the meeting arrive once the decisions are already made.
std
III.B.2
An engineer must tell a senior colleague that his test method gave misleading results. Which approach shows the most tact?
Point out the error at the staff meeting so everyone learns
Discuss the data with him privately, focusing on the method
Say nothing and quietly correct the results herself
Email the colleague’s manager describing the mistake

Tact means delivering a difficult message honestly while preserving the other person’s dignity, so a private, data-focused talk is best. Raising it in public may be accurate but embarrasses the colleague needlessly.
std
III.B.2
A quality manager feels her anger rising as a customer accuses her team of hiding test data. What is the best way to handle the moment?
Pause, keep a calm tone and ask what led to the concern
Defend the team firmly so the customer drops the accusation
End the call and reply later in a formal written statement
Agree with the customer quickly so that the call calms down
Recognizing her own emotion and choosing a calm, curious response keeps the conversation productive and surfaces the real issue. Agreeing to calm things down concedes a claim she has not examined.
std
III.B.2
A new operator proposes a process change that a veteran engineer doubts will work. Which response is most open-minded?
Explain why similar ideas have failed before and move on
Thank the operator and say engineering will handle it
Ask him to bring the idea back when he has more experience
Ask what the operator has observed and how the idea would work

Open-minded, non-judgmental communication explores the idea before judging it, and the operator may have seen something the engineer has not. Citing past failures dismisses the idea without hearing it.
std
III.B.2
A manager notices that team members from some cultures rarely disagree openly in meetings. What is the most culturally responsive approach?
Require each person to state one objection in every meeting
Treat their silence as agreement and move the decision ahead
Offer other channels, such as one-on-one talks or written input
Ask those members to adapt to the meeting’s direct style
Offering several ways to contribute lets people raise concerns in ways that fit their norms. Treating silence as agreement risks missing objections that were never voiced.
std
III.B.2
A quality manager is revising a work instruction for a diverse workforce that includes people with limited English. Which writing practice helps most?
Formal technical terms so that the meaning stays precise
Short sentences, plain words and pictures for key steps
Long paragraphs that explain the theory behind each step
Many abbreviations to keep the instruction to a single page
Plain language and visuals make instructions usable by the widest range of readers. Technical terms may be precise for experts but block understanding for many users.
std
III.B.2
A team keeps proposing fixes before it understands a recurring defect. Which question would best open dialog about the cause?
“What do you see happening just before the defect appears?”
“Don’t you think the operators are causing this problem?”
“Should we simply add an inspection step after this one?”
“Who approved the last change made to this process?”
An open question invites observations and moves the team from solutions to understanding. The question about operators is leading: it suggests an answer and puts people on the defensive.
std
III.B.3
A US quality manager working with a supplier team from a high-context culture finds that his direct written requests get polite agreement but little action. What should he do?
Write the requests more bluntly and add firm deadlines
Escalate to the team’s senior leader without delay
Copy more people so that the requests are widely seen
Build the relationship and confirm understanding in conversation

In high-context cultures meaning rests on relationships and context, so trust and spoken confirmation matter more than the written word. Blunter writing leans harder on the low-context style that is not working.
std
III.B.3
A US team expects a supplier abroad to agree to a corrective action plan in a single meeting, but the supplier’s managers say they must consult others first. What is the best interpretation?
The supplier is stalling and should be placed on probation
The supplier’s managers lack authority and should be replaced
Local decisions may need consensus or senior approval first
The plan is flawed and must be rewritten before any review

Business practices differ in how decisions are made, and many cultures expect consensus or approval from senior leaders. Treating the delay as stalling misreads a normal practice and damages the relationship.
std
III.B.4
After the company put all procedures, data and dashboards online, managers say they spend hours sorting through messages and reports. What should be done?
Add more reports so that every possible question is covered
Tailor what each role receives and highlight the key measures
Go back to paper reports to reduce the amount of information
Send the complete data set to every manager once a week
Technology makes information widely available but can cause overload, so content should be filtered to what each role needs. Adding reports worsens the overload instead of relieving it.
std
III.C.1
Which document formally authorizes a project and names its sponsor, objectives, scope and high-level budget?
Project charter
Work breakdown structure
Gantt chart
Lessons learned register
The charter is produced in initiation and gives the project formal authority. The work breakdown structure comes later, in planning, and breaks the approved scope into work packages.
std
III.C.1
A project charter has just been approved. What happens next, in the planning phase?
Start building deliverables to show the sponsor quick progress
Hand over the deliverables and release the project team
Measure performance against the approved baseline
Define scope, schedule, budget, risks and resources in a plan
Planning turns the charter into a baseline for scope, schedule, cost, risk and resources. Measuring against the baseline is monitoring and controlling, which cannot start until the baseline exists.
std
III.C.1
Which activity belongs mainly to the execution phase of a project?
Writing the business case and getting sponsor approval
Comparing progress with the baseline and correcting variances
Directing the team as it produces the planned deliverables
Archiving project records and capturing lessons learned

Execution is where the team carries out the plan and produces the deliverables. Comparing progress with the baseline is monitoring and controlling, which runs alongside execution but is a separate process group.
std
III.C.1
A project team holds weekly reviews comparing completed work and spending with the baseline and approves corrective actions. Which phase do these reviews represent?
Execution
Monitoring and controlling
Planning
Initiation
Tracking performance against the baseline and acting on variances is monitoring and controlling. Execution produces the work; it does not judge the work against the plan.
std
III.C.1
Midway through a project, the sponsor asks to add a feature without changing the end date or the budget. What should the project manager explain?
Added scope affects time, cost or quality, so a trade-off is needed
The team can absorb the feature by working extra overtime
Scope changes are not allowed once execution has begun
The feature can be added if it is left out of the plan

Scope, time and cost are linked, so adding scope without more time or money puts quality or delivery at risk; the trade-off must be agreed through change control. Changes are allowed during execution if they go through that process.
std
III.C.1
A project to install a new heat-treat furnace has fixed requirements, required permits and a set physical sequence of work. Which methodology fits best?
Iterative, with re-planning every two weeks
Evolutionary, putting a partial furnace into use early
Informal, with no plan so the team stays flexible
Linear, with phases completed in order
Stable requirements and a fixed build sequence suit a linear (waterfall) approach. Iterative methods pay off when requirements are uncertain, which is not the case for a defined installation.
std
III.C.1
A team builds an internal complaint-tracking app. It releases a basic version with core functions, then adds capabilities over several releases based on how people use it. Which approach is this?
Linear
Critical path
Evolutionary
Phase-gate

An evolutionary approach delivers a working core early and grows the product through successive releases as needs become clear. A linear approach would fix all requirements first and deliver once at the end.
std
III.C.2
A proposed training program will cost $40,000 and yield $100,000 in benefits, both in present-value terms. What is its benefit-cost ratio, and what does it show?
0.4, so costs exceed benefits
2.5, so benefits exceed costs
1.5, so benefits exceed costs
0.6, so costs exceed benefits

The benefit-cost ratio is benefits divided by costs: 100,000 ÷ 40,000 = 2.5, and a ratio above 1 means benefits exceed costs. 1.5 divides net benefit by cost, which is a return measure, not the ratio.
std
III.C.2
A sponsor wants one simple visual showing when each task starts and ends and how each is progressing against its dates. Which tool fits best?
Gantt chart
Work breakdown structure
Risk assessment matrix
Benefit-cost analysis
A Gantt chart shows tasks as bars on a timeline and can show progress against planned dates. A work breakdown structure lists the work but has no time scale.
std
III.C.2
A project manager needs the most accurate cost estimate for a project whose work is already well defined. Which approach should she use?
Use the total cost of the last project, whatever its scope
Ask the sponsor what budget is available and use that figure
Add a 50% margin to a top-down guess so the budget is safe
Estimate each work package and roll the costs up

Bottom-up estimating from the WBS work packages is the most accurate method once the work is well defined. Reusing a past project’s total is a quick analogy estimate and is less accurate when scopes differ.
std
III.D.1
A quality department is drafting its mission statement. What should the statement describe?
Numeric targets for defects and returns for the coming year
The detailed procedures for inspection and product testing
Its purpose and how it serves the organization’s mission and customers
The reporting lines and headcount of the quality staff
A quality mission states why the function exists and how it supports the wider mission and its customers. Numeric targets are objectives that flow from the mission and policy, not the mission itself.
std
III.D.3
A quality manager’s dashboard tracks only scrap and defect rates, and leadership asks for a balanced scorecard. What should be added?
Scrap and defect rates broken out by shift, line and product
Financial, customer and learning and growth measures
Only financial measures, since they reflect all other results
Attendance and overtime figures for each department

The balanced scorecard of Kaplan and Norton has financial, customer, internal process and learning and growth perspectives; scrap and defects already cover internal process. Finer breakdowns of scrap add detail but stay in that one perspective.
std
III.D.3
Internal audits have found no nonconformities for three years, yet customer complaints are rising. What should the quality manager suspect?
The audit program may lack depth, risk focus or independence
The system is effective and the complaints reflect customer error
Audits add no value and the program should be suspended
Complaints fall outside the scope of the quality system

Clean audits alongside worsening results suggest the audits are not probing the processes that matter or the auditors are not independent enough. Blaming customers ignores clear external evidence that the system is not working.
std
III.D.3
A customer satisfaction survey drew a 6% response rate, mostly from customers who recently had problems. How should the results be used?
As a reliable measure, since each response came from a real customer
Discarded, since any survey containing complaints is invalid
As proof that satisfaction is low across the whole customer base
With caution, checked against other data, since nonresponse bias is likely

A low, self-selected response may not represent all customers, so the results should be confirmed with other data such as complaints and returns. Treating it as proof of low satisfaction overgeneralizes from a biased sample.
std
III.E.1
A company measures delivery only by its own ship date, while customers judge delivery by the date goods arrive. Which quality management principle is it overlooking?
Process approach
Leadership
Customer focus
Relationship management

Customer focus means understanding and meeting customer requirements, including how customers measure performance. Relationship management concerns managing relationships with interested parties such as suppliers, not defining measures from the customer’s view.
std
III.E.1
Under the ISO 9000 leadership principle, what should top management do?
Delegate all responsibility for the QMS to the quality manager
Set unity of purpose and direction and conditions for people to engage
Personally approve every decision about nonconforming product
Focus on financial results and leave quality to the QMS team

The leadership principle calls on leaders at all levels to establish unity of purpose and direction and create conditions in which people engage in achieving quality objectives. Delegating everything to the quality manager is the opposite of leadership commitment.
std
III.E.1
A plant wants to apply the engagement of people principle. Which action fits best?
Give staff authority and recognition to improve their own work
Post the quality policy in every break room and hallway
Require all employees to attend a yearly ISO 9001 overview
Have the quality department make all improvement decisions
Engagement of people means competent, empowered and recognized people at all levels. Posting the policy communicates it but does not by itself involve anyone.
std
III.E.1
Each department manages its own steps well, yet orders stall at the handoffs between departments. Which quality management principle would help most?
Evidence-based decision making
Customer focus
Leadership
Process approach

The process approach manages activities as interrelated processes that form a system, which targets the handoffs between departments. Better data would show the delays, but the underlying fix is managing the end-to-end process.
std
III.E.1
After winning a quality award, management declares the QMS finished and freezes all processes as they are. Which principle does this conflict with most directly?
Process approach
Relationship management
Improvement
Engagement of people

The improvement principle holds that successful organizations keep an ongoing focus on improvement. The process approach concerns how activities are managed as a system, not whether they keep improving.
std
III.E.1
A company runs joint improvement projects with key suppliers and shares its demand forecasts with them. Which principle is it applying?
Customer focus
Relationship management
Engagement of people
Leadership
Relationship management means managing relationships with interested parties such as suppliers for sustained success. Engagement of people refers to the organization’s own staff, not its suppliers.
std
III.E.2
A team makes many small, low-cost changes to its process each week, led by the people who do the work. Which approach is this?
Kaizen
Business process reengineering
Benchmarking
Final inspection
Kaizen is continuous, incremental improvement driven by the people closest to the work. Reengineering seeks radical redesign through large breakthrough changes, the opposite of small weekly steps.
std
III.E.3

A quality engineer separates variation into chance causes inherent in the process and assignable causes traced to specific events, and plots the data against control limits. Whose work is this based on?
Crosby
Feigenbaum
Juran
Shewhart
Shewhart developed the control chart and the distinction between chance and assignable causes of variation. Crosby is known for zero defects and the cost of nonconformance, not statistical control.
std
III.E.3
A company trains front-line workers in the seven basic quality tools, forms quality circles and uses cause-and-effect diagrams. Whose ideas is it applying?
Crosby
Shewhart
Ishikawa
Feigenbaum

Ishikawa promoted quality circles, the seven basic tools for all workers and the cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram. Feigenbaum originated total quality control but is not associated with quality circles or the fishbone.
std
IV.A.1
A team flowcharts its invoice approval process and finds three loops where invoices are sent back to the requester. How should the team use this output?
Treat the loops as likely rework and delay, and find out why invoices are sent back
Remove the loops from the chart so that it shows the intended process
Count the boxes on the chart to estimate the cost of each invoice
Add an approval step before each loop to catch errors sooner
Loops on a flowchart point to rework, which adds cost and delay, so they are prime targets for study. Adding approval steps adds more checking without removing the reason invoices are rejected.
std
IV.A.1
A supervisor wants to know whether day-to-day changes in fill weight reflect real process changes or only routine variation, and to keep watching the process over time. Which tool fits?
Frequency histogram
Control chart
Pareto chart
Check sheet

A control chart plots data in time order against limits based on the process's own variation, separating signals from routine noise. A histogram shows the spread but loses the time order, so it cannot show when a change happened.
std
IV.A.1
A defect-location check sheet shows nearly all paint runs marked in the lower left corner of the panel. What does this output most usefully suggest?
More panels should be checked before any cause is studied
The panels should be inspected twice as often from now on
Something about how that area is sprayed, racked or drained is causing the runs
The paint itself is out of specification and should be returned

A location check sheet is meant to reveal clusters, and a tight cluster points to a cause tied to that spot, such as gun angle or racking. A bad batch of paint would cause runs all over the panel, and collecting more data or inspecting more often delays action without finding the cause.
std
IV.A.2
A team has the broad goal “cut customer onboarding time” and needs to break it down, level by level, into specific actions that can be assigned to owners. Which tool fits?
Affinity diagram
Interrelationship digraph
Activity network diagram
Tree diagram
A tree diagram breaks a goal into successively finer means until actions are specific enough to assign. An affinity diagram works the other way, grouping many loose ideas into themes.
std
IV.A.2
A team wants to show, in one grid, which of 12 customer requirements each of 8 process steps addresses, and how strongly. Which tool fits?
Matrix diagram
Tree diagram
Process decision program chart
Affinity diagram
A matrix diagram shows the presence and strength of relationships between two or more sets of items. A tree diagram breaks one item into parts but does not cross two lists against each other.
std
IV.A.2
In an activity network, A (3 days) starts the project; B (5 days) and C (2 days) follow A; D (4 days) follows C; E (1 day) follows both B and D. What is the critical path and project length?
A-B-E, 9 days
A-C-D-E, 10 days
A-B-C-D-E, 15 days
A-C-D-E, 9 days

Path A-B-E takes 3 + 5 + 1 = 9 days and path A-C-D-E takes 3 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 10 days; the longest path sets the project length. Adding every activity to get 15 days ignores that B runs in parallel with C and D.
std
IV.A.3
A team has named a likely root cause for a recurring hydraulic leak. Before committing money to the corrective action, what should it do?
Vote on the cause that most team members feel is right
Have the department head sign off on the named cause
Confirm with data that the leak follows the suspected cause
Proceed, since the cause came out of a fishbone session

A suspected root cause should be verified, ideally by showing the problem can be turned on and off with it, before resources are spent. Votes and sign-offs measure agreement, not whether the cause is real.
std
IV.A.3
A team piloted a new scheduling method on one line, compared the results with its prediction and confirmed the improvement. Under PDCA, what comes next?
Do: run the same pilot again on the same line
Plan: rewrite the problem statement and set new improvement goals
Check: collect baseline data on the old method
Act: standardize the method and decide how to extend it

Comparing results with the prediction completes Check; Act adopts and standardizes what worked and decides on wider use, then the cycle turns again. Repeating the pilot adds delay without new learning once the result is confirmed.
std
IV.A.3
A six sigma team has statistically confirmed the main causes of invoice errors and is now generating, selecting and piloting solutions. Which DMAIC phase is it in?
Improve
Analyze
Control
Measure
Generating, choosing and piloting solutions is the work of Improve. Analyze is where the causes were found and confirmed, which the team has already finished.
std
IV.A.3
At the start of a project, a team needs a one-page view of the process's boundaries: who provides what, the five to seven main steps, what is produced and who receives it. Which tool fits?
Value stream map
SIPOC diagram
Detailed swim-lane flowchart
Failure mode and effects analysis

A SIPOC is the standard high-level scoping tool, listing suppliers, inputs, process steps, outputs and customers. A value stream map adds timing, inventory and information flow and comes later, once the scope is set.
std
IV.A.3
A corrective action for mislabeled shipments was put in place three months ago. Before the CAPA is closed, what still needs to be confirmed?
That the revised procedure was approved and issued
That all affected staff signed the training record
That data show the mislabeling has not recurred
That the customer accepted the root cause report
Closing a CAPA requires evidence that the action was effective, meaning the nonconformity has not recurred. Issued procedures and training records show the action was carried out, not that it worked.
std
IV.A.3

A manager asks a team to summarize its work on one large sheet: background, current condition, goal, root cause analysis, countermeasures, plan and follow-up. What is a main purpose of this A3 format?
To replace data analysis with the shared judgment of the team
To act as the binding contract for supplier corrective action
To record only the final solution that management approved
To show the problem-solving logic so that others can follow and challenge it

An A3 tells the whole PDCA story on one page so that reviewers can test the reasoning from problem to countermeasure. It relies on data rather than replacing analysis, and it records the path, not just the final answer.
std
IV.A.4
A product manager, working alone, wants to explore ideas radiating from the central theme “customer onboarding” and see how subtopics connect, without forcing a sequence. Which technique fits?
Mind mapping
Activity network diagram
Pareto analysis
Five whys analysis

A mind map places a theme at the center and branches out to related ideas and sub-ideas freely, which suits individual exploration. An activity network imposes a sequence of tasks, which is what the manager wants to avoid.
std
IV.A.4
A facilitator asks a team stuck on clinic waiting times, “What if patients did not need to wait in the clinic at all?” and uses random-word prompts to spark ideas. Which approach is this?
Critical thinking
Lateral thinking
Root cause analysis
Nominal group technique

Lateral thinking, associated with Edward de Bono, uses provocations and random entry points to escape the usual line of reasoning. Critical thinking evaluates claims and evidence rather than generating unconventional ideas.
std
IV.A.4
A software vendor claims its product cut defects 40 percent at a client site. A manager applying critical thinking would first:
Accept the figure, since the vendor has a strong reputation
Generate many alternative ideas without judging any of them
Ask how the figure was measured and what else changed at that site
Rank the claim against other vendors' published claims by size of gain
Critical thinking tests a claim's evidence, measurement and alternative explanations before accepting it. Generating ideas without judgment is brainstorming, which does not evaluate the claim at all.
std
IV.A.5
Which of these is an appraisal cost?
Reworking assemblies that fail final test
Supplier quality planning before a first order
Replacing defective units under warranty
Inspecting incoming material from suppliers
Appraisal costs are spent measuring and evaluating conformance, such as receiving inspection. Rework of units caught in the plant is internal failure, and up-front supplier planning is prevention.
std
IV.A.5
A product passes all plant tests, but a customer rejects a shipment for a defect, and the company pays return freight and a contract penalty. How should these costs be classified?
External failure
Internal failure
Appraisal
Prevention
Costs that arise after the product reaches the customer, such as returns and penalties, are external failure costs. Internal failure covers defects found before shipment, which this was not.
std
IV.B.2

A process analysis of loan approvals finds that an application is actively worked on for about 2 hours in total but spends 8 days waiting between departments. Where is the greatest opportunity to cut cycle time?
Speed up the 2 hours of hands-on processing work
Cut the waiting time between departments
Add staff to the step with the most work content
Add an extra review step to catch errors earlier
Almost all of the cycle time is waiting, a non-value-added waste, so removing queues and handoffs gives by far the largest gain. Even halving the 2 hours of work would barely change an 8-day cycle.
std
IV.B.3
A team starting 5S in a crowded tool room asks where to begin. What should the first step be?
Paint floor lines and label every shelf location
Clean all equipment and check its condition
Remove items not needed for current work
Write audit checklists for the supervisors to use
Sort comes first: removing what is not needed frees space and avoids organizing clutter. Labeling locations is Set in order, which only makes sense once unneeded items are gone.
std
IV.B.3
A plant moves to just-in-time delivery from a supplier with a poor on-time and quality record. What risk does this create most directly?
Higher holding cost from the larger safety stock that JIT requires
Overproduction, since JIT pushes parts to the line well ahead of actual need
Longer changeovers, since JIT requires larger production batches
Line stoppages, since little inventory is left to absorb late or bad lots

JIT strips out buffer stock, so it depends on reliable suppliers; problems that inventory once hid now stop the line. JIT reduces safety stock rather than adding it, so higher holding cost is the opposite of what happens.
std
IV.B.3
Compared with a detailed flowchart of a single department's steps, what is a value stream map mainly used to do?
Show material and information flow across the whole stream, with time data
List every keystroke and form field used inside one department
Rank defect categories by how often each one occurs in the plant
Assign individual operators to specific work cells according to their skill level

A value stream map follows a product family end to end, showing material and information flow, inventory, and process and lead times so that waste across the stream can be seen. Ranking defect categories is a Pareto chart's job.
std
IV.B.3
A plant manager wants to use a kaizen event to cut setup time on one press. Which approach is consistent with kaizen?
An engineering group designs a new press over the next year
Operators and support staff make quick, practical changes in a focused week
Consultants write a recommendation for later management review
Operators are handed the new setup-time target and left to meet it on their own

A kaizen event brings a cross-functional team, including the people who do the work, to make rapid, low-cost improvements and test them on the spot. A year-long redesign is a large capital project, not kaizen.
std
IV.B.3
Training Within Industry's Job Instruction method teaches a supervisor to train an operator on a standard job by:
Handing over the written instruction and checking the output a week later
Having the learner watch an experienced operator for a full shift
Preparing the learner, presenting the steps, having the learner try, then following up
Showing a video of the job and testing the learner with a written quiz

Job Instruction uses four steps: prepare the worker, present the operation, try out performance and follow up. Shadowing an experienced operator passes on that person's habits, good and bad, instead of the standard method.
std
IV.B.3
Which set makes up the three basic elements of standard work?
Cycle time, inspection frequency and control limits
Lead time, batch size and finished goods safety stock
Work sequence, quality targets and incentive pay rates
Takt time, work sequence and standard work-in-process

Standard work is built on takt time, the sequence of work elements and the standard in-process stock needed to keep flow. Control limits and inspection plans belong to process control, not to the definition of standard work.
std
IV.B.3
Under total productive maintenance, operators take on daily cleaning, lubrication, tightening and inspection of their own machines. What is this pillar called?
Autonomous maintenance
Planned maintenance
Breakdown maintenance
Predictive maintenance
Autonomous maintenance gives operators routine care of their equipment so that abnormal conditions are found early. Planned maintenance is the scheduled work done by the maintenance department.
std
IV.B.4
Goldratt compares an organization to a chain. What does this imply for improvement?
Strengthening any one link raises the whole chain's strength in proportion
Output is limited by the weakest link, so improvement should focus there
Every link should be strengthened by an equal amount at once
Each link should be measured and rewarded on its own efficiency
A chain is only as strong as its weakest link, so effort spent elsewhere adds little to system output. Rewarding each link's own efficiency is the local optimization that TOC warns against.
std
IV.B.4
Using a TOC current reality tree, a team traces late shipments, heavy overtime and constant expediting back to one scheduling policy. In TOC terms, how are these classified?
The policy is an undesirable effect; the others are core problems
The policy is a physical constraint on the plant's capacity
The policy is a core problem; the others are undesirable effects
The policy is solution deterioration; the others are constraints

Undesirable effects are the visible symptoms, and the core problem is the common cause that produces most of them. Because the issue is a rule rather than limited equipment, it is not a physical constraint.
std
IV.B.4

Two years ago a plant broke its paint-line constraint, partly by changing its batching rules. Throughput has since stalled; the constraint has moved to assembly, but rules built around paint are still in force. Which TOC idea does this show?
A physical constraint that remains at the paint line
An undesirable effect caused by low operator skill
Local optimization of the assembly department at the expense of the plant
Solution deterioration through inertia after the constraint moved

When a constraint is broken, the system's needs change, and rules that once helped can become the new limit if no one revisits them; TOC's fifth focusing step warns against this inertia. The paint line is no longer the constraint, so treating it as one is wrong.
std
IV.C.1
A team plans to change a process next month and wants to show whether the change worked. When should it start collecting data on the key output?
Now, to set a baseline first
Right after the change, to see the new level
Only if complaints rise after the change
At year-end, when annual totals are complete
Without a baseline taken before the change, there is nothing to compare the new results against. Measuring only after the change shows the new level but cannot show improvement.
std
IV.C.3
Six readings are 12, 15, 15, 18, 20 and 22. What are the mode and the range?
Mode 16.5, range 10
Mode 15, range 10
Mode 15, range 22
Mode 17, range 10
The mode is the most frequent value, 15, and the range is the largest minus the smallest, 22 - 12 = 10. A mode of 16.5 is the median and 17 is the mean.
std
IV.C.3
A sample has three readings: 3, 5 and 7. What is the sample variance?
The mean is 5, the squared deviations sum to 4 + 0 + 4 = 8, and dividing by n - 1 = 2 gives 4. Dividing by n gives the population figure of 2.67, and 2 is the standard deviation.
std
IV.C.3
Fill weights are roughly normally distributed with a mean of 50 g and a standard deviation of 2 g. About what share of fills fall between 46 g and 54 g?
68 percent
99.7 percent
50 percent
95 percent
46 to 54 g is the mean plus or minus two standard deviations, which holds about 95 percent of a normal distribution. 68 percent is the share within one standard deviation.
std
IV.C.3
What does a run chart show that a histogram of the same data does not?
The time order of the data, so trends and shifts can be seen
Control limits calculated from the process variation
The overall shape of the distribution of the data
Specification limits for judging the capability of the process

A run chart plots values in time order around a center line such as the median, revealing trends, shifts and cycles. It has no statistically calculated control limits; adding those makes it a control chart.
std
IV.C.4
In measurement terms, what does accuracy describe?
Closeness of repeated readings to one another
Closeness to the true or reference value
The smallest increment the gauge can display
Steadiness of readings over a long period
Accuracy concerns closeness to the true or reference value. Agreement among repeated readings is precision, and a measurement system can be precise yet inaccurate.
std
IV.C.5
Bore diameters rise and fall in a regular pattern that repeats every fourth subgroup, matching the rotation among four fixtures. How is this pattern best described?
A seasonal pattern tied to the time of year
A gradual trend caused by steady tool wear
A cyclical pattern tied to a recurring factor
A single sustained shift in the process mean level
A regular, repeating rise and fall linked to a recurring cause such as fixture rotation is a cycle. A seasonal pattern follows the calendar, which a four-subgroup repeat does not.
std
IV.C.5
Coating thickness readings run high on humid afternoons and low on dry mornings, and the changes track the plant's humidity log. What should the team do?
Treat the swings as routine noise, since they happen every day
Recalculate the control limits so that the humid readings fall inside
Adjust the coater after every high reading to bring it back to target
Treat humidity as a cause and test controlling or offsetting it
A pattern that tracks an outside condition points to an environmental cause that can be controlled or offset. Widening limits to absorb it hides a known, assignable cause instead of removing it.
std
IV.C.8
After years of low, steady failure rates, a fleet of pumps starts failing more often as bearings reach the end of their life. On the bathtub curve, which phase is this?
Wear-out, as failure rate rises with age
Infant mortality, where early weak units fail
Useful life, where failures occur at random
Burn-in, where units are screened before use
The rising right-hand side of the bathtub curve is wear-out, when aging drives failures up. Useful life is the flat middle region of low, roughly constant failure rate that the pumps have just left.
std
IV.C.8
A repairable machine's mean time between failures rises from 200 to 400 operating hours. What does this mean?
Each repair now takes about half as long as it did before
On average, it now runs twice as long between failures
It will now last 400 hours before it wears out
All failures in the first 400 hours are removed
MTBF is the average operating time between failures of a repairable item, so doubling it means failures are half as frequent. Repair time is measured by MTTR, not MTBF.
std
IV.C.8
Early in design, a team estimates reliability against a customer requirement of 95 percent of units surviving the warranty period. What is the main value of doing this?
Replacing prototype and field testing with calculation alone
Setting the warranty price only after the product launches
Finding gaps against the requirement while design changes are cheap
Proving that no units of the product will ever fail in the field

Early estimates show whether the design can meet the requirement while changes still cost little, guiding test plans and design choices. Estimates complement testing rather than replace it, and no estimate can prove zero failures.
std
IV.C.8
Process reliability is defined as net production x 100 / (scheduled time x target production rate). What does this measure compare?
The average time between failures with the average time to repair them
The number of units that pass inspection with the number inspected
The scheduled production time with the total calendar time available
Actual net output with what the line should make at target rate in the scheduled time

The denominator is what the line would produce running at its target rate for all scheduled time, so the ratio shows how much of that potential was actually delivered. MTBF and MTTR are separate equipment measures, not this ratio.
std
IV.C.8
Installation and operational qualification of a new sealing line are complete. What does process (performance) qualification then show?
That the process consistently makes conforming product under normal production conditions
That the equipment was installed to the supplier's drawings and specifications
That each machine function works correctly across its specified ranges
That every operator on the line has passed the required training tests

Performance or process qualification shows that the process, run as it will be in production, consistently yields conforming product. Testing functions across their ranges is operational qualification, which is already done.
std
V.A.2
A snack maker sells to grocery chains, which resell its products to consumers. Which statement best describes how these external customers shape the product?
Chains set packaging and delivery needs; consumers set taste and value needs
Only the grocery chains matter, because they are the ones who pay the invoices
Consumers set every requirement, and the chains simply pass the orders through
Neither group shapes it, since engineering sets the product specification alone

Both the direct buyer and the end user are external customers, and each brings different requirements to the product and its delivery. Treating only the paying chain as the customer ignores the consumer whose purchases drive the chain's orders.
std
V.A.3
An analysis shows 15% of a distributor's accounts produce 70% of its profit, while 30% of accounts lose money once service costs are included. How should this shape segmentation?
Close all of the money-losing accounts at once to raise the overall profit margin
Segment accounts by value and match service level and cost to serve to each tier
Treat every account the same so that no customer feels it is valued any less
Move the most profitable accounts to self-service so as to cut their cost to serve

Value-based segmentation lets the organization protect its most valuable customers and serve the others at a cost that fits what they are worth. Dropping every unprofitable account at once ignores options such as lower-cost service models and the future value of those accounts.
std
V.A.4
Survey ratings for a bank's new self-service kiosks are only slightly below target, but branch staff say customers struggle with them. Which method would best show what customers find difficult?
Count the kiosk transactions completed at each branch on every business day
Add a survey question asking customers to rate the kiosks on a 1 to 10 scale
Observe customers at the kiosks and record where they hesitate or ask for help
Ask the kiosk vendor for its uptime and error-code report for the last quarter

Observation records capture what customers actually do, including problems they would not think to report on a survey. Another rating question repeats the summary score already available and still does not say where customers get stuck.
std
V.A.4
A focus group of eight customers strongly prefers a new package design, and the marketing director wants to report that most customers prefer it. How should the quality manager respond?
Accept the claim, since a focus group gives objective results for the market
Discard the results, because opinions from a focus group have no real value
Repeat the focus group with the same eight people to confirm the finding
Treat it as insight into reasons, and test it with a larger survey

Focus groups are good at revealing why customers feel as they do, but a small, non-random group cannot be projected to the whole market. A survey of a larger sample can test how widespread the preference is; discarding the insight wastes it.
std
V.B.1
Laptop buyers say they want a battery that will 'last all day.' In quality function deployment, what should the team do with this statement?
Translate it into a measurable target such as battery hours in typical use
List it as a technical characteristic in exactly the words customers used
Leave it out because it is too vague to place in the house of quality
Replace it with the largest battery that fits inside the current case design

QFD keeps the customer's words as a requirement and translates it into measurable technical characteristics with target values. Dropping vague statements loses real needs, and jumping to a design solution skips deciding what must be measured.
std
V.B.1
Market research and QFD show that customers for an industrial valve now need a higher pressure rating than the one in an existing long-term supply contract. What should the supplier do?
Build the higher rating into valves shipped under the contract without telling anyone
Review the change with the customer and amend the contract requirements as agreed
Keep shipping to the old rating, since the signed terms override any changing needs
Stop all shipments until the customer issues a new contract with the higher rating

When customer needs change, the contractual requirements should be reviewed and changed with the customer so both parties agree on what will be supplied. Changing the product without agreement creates unapproved deviations, and ignoring the new need risks losing the customer.
std
V.B.2
Field service technicians hear customer praise and complaints every day, but none of it is recorded. What would make them an effective listening post?
Ask them to pass every comment on to the customer's sales representative by phone
Replace their comments with an annual survey sent to the same set of customers
Give them a simple way to log comments and route the log for regular trend review
Record only the comments that the technicians judge to be formal complaints

A listening post works when feedback captured at a point of customer contact is recorded and analyzed. Logging only formal complaints throws away positive feedback and early warnings, and informal phone relays leave no data to trend.
std
V.B.2
Satisfaction scores for a restaurant chain's online ordering have dropped, but the survey comment fields say little. Which tool would best uncover the reasons?
A larger mailing of the same survey to more online customers
A count of online orders per store compared with last year
A review of the website's server uptime logs for the period
A moderated focus group of recent online ordering customers
A moderated focus group can probe why customers are less satisfied and draw out issues they did not write down. Sending the same survey to more people would confirm the drop but still not explain it.
std
V.B.2
A quality manager uses warranty claims to judge customer satisfaction with a home appliance. What is a key limitation of this data?
It misses unclaimed problems and arrives months after the build
It cannot be linked to production dates, so it gives no clue to the cause
It measures only delivery performance and not the product's performance
It overstates problems, since customers claim for every minor annoyance

Warranty data are a lagging measure and include only failures that customers report within the warranty period. Claims usually can be traced to build dates, which is one of their strengths for finding causes.
std
V.B.2
A company emails its satisfaction survey only to customers whose service tickets were closed as resolved, and scores are very high. What is the main problem?
Email surveys tend to draw fewer replies than surveys conducted over the phone
Leaving out unresolved customers biases the sample and overstates satisfaction
The scores are too high to be useful, so the rating scale should be widened
Resolved customers judge the service more harshly than other customers do

A survey sample must represent the customers whose satisfaction is being judged, and excluding those with unresolved problems removes the least satisfied. Response rate by channel is a lesser concern that does not explain the bias.
std
V.B.2
A customer complains that a shipment arrived with crushed cartons, and the quality manager replaces the goods the next day. What else is needed for an effective corrective action?
Send the customer a discount coupon to use against the next order placed
Ask the freight carrier to sign a letter promising more care next time
Find and remove the cause of the damage and verify that it does not recur
Close the complaint, since the customer has now received good replacement goods

Replacing the goods is a correction that fixes this instance; corrective action removes the cause and checks that it worked. A coupon or a carrier's promise does nothing to find out why the cartons were crushed.
std
V.B.2
A subscription software firm wants to keep customers before they decide to cancel. Which approach is the most proactive?
Offer a discount to customers after they submit a cancellation notice
Survey former customers each year to ask why they chose to cancel
Raise prices for new customers to make up for the revenue that is lost
Watch usage data for early signs of risk and contact those accounts

Spotting warning signs such as falling usage and reaching out before the customer decides is proactive retention. Surveying former customers is useful for learning, but it reacts after the customer is already gone.
std
V.B.3
Patient surveys at a clinic rate the clinical care highly but describe front-desk staff as curt and unwelcoming. What is the most effective response?
Set courtesy standards for the desk, train staff, and coach them on the job
Post a sign asking patients to be patient with the busy front-desk staff
Remove the front-desk questions from future patient surveys to focus on care
Add clinical staff, since the quality of care drives patient loyalty

Courtesy is a service principle that can be defined, trained and reinforced like any other requirement. Adding clinical staff addresses an area customers already rate well and leaves the front-desk problem untouched.
std
V.B.3
A caterer is praised for its food, but customers complain that orders often arrive missing utensils or with the wrong meal count. Which principle is failing, and what helps most?
Rapid response; deliver orders earlier so that any gaps can be fixed
Attention to detail; verify each order against a checklist before dispatch
Empathy; train drivers to apologize warmly when an item is missing
Easy access; add a phone line that customers can call about any missing items

Missing items and wrong counts are failures of attention to detail, and a pre-dispatch check prevents them. Earlier delivery or a call line only helps customers recover from errors that should not have occurred.
std
V.B.3
A customer calls a utility, upset that its billing error caused an overdraft at her bank. Which agent response best shows empathy?
Explaining that billing errors are rare and affect very few accounts
Transferring her quickly to billing so a specialist can review it
Acknowledging how stressful the overdraft must be, then explaining the fix
Reading out the billing dispute policy and the deadline for filing a formal claim

Empathy means recognizing the customer's situation and feelings before moving to the solution. Saying errors are rare minimizes her experience, and an immediate transfer may be efficient but does not acknowledge her at all.
std
V.B.4

Two major customers buying the same standard component ask for conflicting changes: one wants a tighter tolerance, the other a price cut that the tighter tolerance would rule out. What should the quality manager recommend?
Make the change requested by whichever customer placed its formal request first
Adopt the tighter tolerance for all and raise the price for both customers
Decline both requests so that neither customer is favored over the other
Weigh both against strategy and capability, then offer variants or trade-offs

Conflicting requirements are resolved by evaluating them against the organization's priorities and capability and then agreeing a solution, such as separate variants, with each customer. First-come rules and blanket refusals ignore the value and needs of the customers involved.
std
VI.B

A supplier risk assessment scores likelihood of disruption and impact on the company, each from 1 to 5. P scores 4 and 2, Q scores 2 and 5, R scores 3 and 3, S scores 1 and 5. Using likelihood times impact, which supplier should get mitigation first?
Supplier P, which has the highest likelihood score of 4
Supplier Q, with a risk score of 10
Supplier R, with a combined risk score of 9
Supplier S, which ties for the highest impact score
Multiplying likelihood by impact gives P 8, Q 10, R 9 and S 5, so Q carries the most risk. Picking P or S looks at only one dimension; R is close but still below Q.
std
VI.B
A resin supplier announces a six-week allocation that will cut its deliveries in half. Before choosing a response, what should the quality manager assess first?
Whether the resin supplier’s ISO 9001 certificate is still current and valid
Whether the purchase contract allows a penalty for the delivery shortfall
How the supplier scored on its most recent annual quality audit
Which products, lines and orders use the resin and how long stock lasts

The response depends on the impact on internal processes: which products and orders are exposed and how much time existing stock buys. Certificates, audit scores and penalties do not tell the company what will stop or when.
std
VI.B
A supplier switches to a new raw material source without telling its customer, and the parts still meet every drawing dimension. Why is this a risk for the customer?
The new source will almost certainly raise the unit price of the part it supplies
The change automatically cancels the supplier’s ISO 9001 certificate for that site
The unvalidated change may affect performance in ways drawing checks miss
The customer loses its right to reject later lots of the part

Drawing dimensions do not capture every property that matters in use, so an unvalidated material change can alter performance undetected; this is why supplier agreements require change notification and approval. The change does not void certification or limit rejection rights.
std
VI.C
A company wants its 40 active suppliers to know how they are performing between annual reviews, without adding meetings. Which approach fits best?
Send an annual letter summarizing each supplier’s overall rating for the year
Contact a supplier only when one of its lots is rejected at receiving
Send each supplier a monthly scorecard of its own quality and delivery data
Ask each supplier to report its own performance figures every quarter

A routine scorecard built from the customer’s own data gives every supplier regular, objective feedback with no extra meetings. An annual letter is too infrequent, reject-only contact gives no overall picture, and self-reported figures may not match what the customer experiences.
std
VI.C
A supplier’s shipments arrive within the agreed week but on random days, causing dock congestion and line shortages at a plant that schedules daily. What should the buyer do first?
Record these shipments as late on the supplier’s monthly delivery scorecard
Set the required day, time window and quantity, and get the supplier to agree
Raise the plant’s safety stock so the day each shipment arrives no longer matters
Issue a formal corrective action request against the supplier’s shipping process

The supplier is meeting the requirement it was given; the requirement itself is too loose. Making the delivery expectation explicit and confirming acceptance fixes the cause. Scoring the shipments late or issuing a corrective action blames the supplier for meeting the agreement.
std
VI.C
A new supplier receives a drawing with tight tolerances and a list of special characteristics. What is the best way to confirm it understands and can meet them before production starts?
Hold a joint feasibility review where it commits to each requirement
Treat its acceptance of the purchase order as proof that it understands
Inspect the first production lot fully when it arrives at receiving
Send a second copy of the drawing with the critical items highlighted

A feasibility or contract review with the supplier surfaces any requirement it cannot meet before parts are made and records its commitment. Accepting the order does not show understanding, and inspecting the first lot finds problems only after they occur.
std
VI.D
A supplier’s motors pass incoming inspection with zero defects, yet warranty returns show many fail in the field during the first year. Which measure should be added to its scorecard?
Rate of lots accepted at incoming inspection
Percentage of shipments delivered on time
PPM rejected during final assembly
Field failure rate in service

The gap is in reliability and functional performance over time, which only field or warranty data reveal. Incoming acceptance and assembly PPM measure conformance at the point of build, which the motors already pass.
std
VI.D

Supplier A prices a part at $10.00 and Supplier B at $9.50. For every 1,000 parts, A causes $200 of sorting, scrap and rework cost and B causes $1,000. Which is cheaper per part on a total cost basis?
Supplier B: $9.50 versus $10.00 for A
Supplier A: $10.20 versus $10.50 for B
Supplier B: $9.60 versus $10.20 for A
Supplier A: $10.00 versus $10.50 for B

Quality cost per part is $200 / 1,000 = $0.20 for A and $1,000 / 1,000 = $1.00 for B, so A costs $10.20 and B $10.50 per part. The first option compares price alone, $9.60 divides B’s quality cost by 10,000 instead of 1,000, and $10.00 drops A’s own quality cost.
std
VI.D
A supplier of programmable controllers ships good units on time, but engineers say its help line takes a week to answer application questions. Which measure would best track this problem?
Percentage of units that pass functional testing at receiving
Median time to resolve engineers’ technical support requests
Number of nonconformance reports raised against its shipments
Percentage of purchase orders acknowledged within two days

The problem is the availability of technical support, so the measure should time support requests from receipt to resolution. Order acknowledgment time measures commercial responsiveness, and the test and nonconformance measures track product quality, which is already good.
std
VI.E

A supplier finds the cause of a defect on one machine. Two other machines of the same design run other parts and have had no defects yet. What should its response include beyond fixing the affected machine?
Extra final inspection on the affected machine until the next audit
A statement that the other machines are fine since they show no defects
Retraining for all of the operators who ran the affected machine
Preventive action to apply the fix to the other two machines

Applying the fix where the same cause could occur, before it does, is preventive action. Relying on the lack of defects so far ignores a known risk, and extra inspection or retraining does not remove the cause.
std
VI.E
After an on-site audit, the auditor has four nonconformities to raise with the supplier. Which feedback practice best supports improvement?
Send the report only to the buyer, who decides whether to share it
Share only the overall audit score so the supplier is not overwhelmed
Go over each finding at the closing meeting and follow with a written report
Wait until the supplier’s next performance review to raise the findings
Prompt, specific feedback backed by evidence lets the supplier understand each finding and act on it. A score alone does not say what to fix, and delaying or filtering the findings slows correction.
std
VI.F
When is a strategic alliance with a supplier most appropriate?
When each firm needs the other’s capabilities for a long-term goal
When the item is a standard commodity available from many sources
When the main aim is to lower the unit price through annual rebidding
When the supplier is new and has no performance record with the firm

Alliances share resources, risk and rewards, which pays off when each side brings something the other needs for a long-term, high-value goal. Standard commodities and price-driven rebidding suit transactional buying.
std
VI.G
Why does a defect in a low-cost purchased part often cost far more than the part itself?
Suppliers often price low and recover the cost through later charges
It is found in assembly or the field, where costs multiply
Incoming inspection costs rise in proportion to each part’s price
The cost of replacing a part is set by the selling price of the product

A cheap part built into an assembly or a shipped product brings teardown, delay, warranty and customer costs that dwarf its price. Inspection cost does not depend on part price, and supplier pricing tactics do not explain the multiplier.
std
VI.G
A hotel outsources its laundry. Linens arrive on time and in full, but some are stained. What is the main impact on the hotel’s service?
Little impact, since laundry is a back-office service guests rarely notice
The impact is limited to the cost of rewashing the stained linens
Guests will direct their complaints to the laundry supplier instead of the hotel
Guests judge the hotel itself, so the supplier’s lapse lowers their view of it
Customers experience the total service package and hold the hotel responsible for every part of it, including outsourced parts. The rewash cost is minor next to the damage to guest satisfaction.
std
VI.G
A receiving inspector finds that the sample from an incoming lot fails the sampling plan. What should happen next?
Tag and segregate the lot, record it and route it for disposition
Release the lot to stock and raise the issue at the supplier’s quarterly review
Draw a second sample and accept the lot if that sample passes
Scrap the lot at once and order replacements from another source

A rejected lot must be identified and kept from use, documented, and dispositioned by those authorized to do so (return, sort, use as is or scrap). Resampling until a sample passes defeats the plan, and immediate scrapping skips disposition.
std
VII.C
When developing a new course, what should the designer write before creating slides and exercises?
The end-of-course reaction survey for participants
Measurable learning objectives from the needs analysis
A detailed schedule of trainer assignments for the year
The description that will appear in the course catalog

Learning objectives drawn from the needs analysis define what learners must be able to do, so content, exercises and tests can be built to match. Surveys, schedules and catalog text follow from the design rather than drive it.
std
VII.C
Which situation is best suited to instructor-led classroom training?
Learners in many time zones need to complete content at their own pace
A single new hire needs to learn a machine-specific setup procedure
A group needs shared content plus discussion and answers to questions
Operators must rehearse rare emergencies on complex equipment

Classroom delivery suits a group that benefits from interaction and immediate answers. Self-paced learners across time zones suit e-learning, a single machine setup suits on-the-job training, and rare emergencies suit simulation.
std
VII.C
Field technicians need training they can work through at their own pace on site, often without internet access, covering troubleshooting steps. Which delivery method fits best?
A structured workbook with worked exercises
A live classroom session at the company headquarters
A web-based e-learning course that needs a connection
A one-time demonstration by a senior technician

A workbook is portable, self-paced and usable offline, and its exercises let technicians practice. E-learning fails without a connection, and a classroom session or one-time demonstration does not fit field schedules or serve as a lasting reference.
std
VII.C
A company must train 3,000 employees in 20 countries on a data privacy policy and keep proof of completion for regulators. Which method fits best?
Classroom sessions run by the legal team in each of the countries
On-the-job training led by each employee’s own supervisor
A policy document emailed to all staff for self-directed reading
Computer-delivered e-learning with a test and tracked completion

Computer-delivered training reaches a large, scattered audience consistently and records completion and test results as evidence. Emailing the policy gives no proof of understanding, and classroom or supervisor-led delivery is costly and hard to keep consistent.
std
VII.C
What is the main limitation of self-directed learning?
It cannot easily be fitted around the learner’s other work duties
It generally costs more per learner than classroom training does
It relies on learner drive and has few checks of understanding
It works only for learners who already hold a college degree

Self-directed learning is flexible and cheap per learner, but progress depends on the learner’s drive and there is little feedback to confirm understanding. Flexibility is its strength, not its weakness.
std

A newly promoted quality engineer has strong technical skills but needs to learn how to work across the organization and plan her career over the next year. Which support fits best?
Coaching from her supervisor on how to run one specific test
A classroom course on the company’s quality procedures
A simulation of difficult customer audit meetings
Mentoring by a senior manager outside her reporting line

Mentoring is a longer-term relationship focused on career growth and organizational know-how, best given by an experienced person outside the reporting line. Coaching on a specific task targets job performance, not the broader development she needs.
